entries.title: Disease burden attributable to intimate partner violence against females and sexual violence against children in 204 countries and territories, 1990-2023: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023.
entries.design: GBD modelling study (systematic analysis, spatiotemporal Gaussian process regression + burden-of-proof risk methodology)
entries.population_setting: 204 countries and territories, females aged 15+ (IPV) and males/females (sexual violence against children), 1990-2023
entries.finding: In 2023, an estimated 608 million (95% UI 518-724) females aged 15+ had ever been exposed to IPV, contributing 18.5 million (8.74-30.0) DALYs; IPV ranked as the 4th leading risk factor for DALYs among females aged 15-49. Anxiety disorders and major depressive disorder were the leading IPV-attributed health outcomes (5.43 million and 3.96 million DALYs respectively).
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly grounds the marriage-transition-as-governance-threshold rationale and the primary-prevention framing of T-PHE by quantifying IPV as a top-tier global disease burden driver; supports the rationale for P1 (decision control as a mechanism worth intervening on) but is a burden-of-disease estimate, not evidence T-PHE itself works.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms verbatim: 608 million (95% UI 518-724) females 15+ ever exposed to IPV; 18.5 million (8.74-30.0) DALYs; IPV ranked 4th (SVAC 5th) leading risk factor for DALYs among females 15-49; anxiety disorders 5.43 million and MDD 3.96 million DALYs. relevance_to_tphe correctly hedges that this is a burden estimate, not evidence T-PHE works.

entries.title: Global, regional, and national prevalence estimates of physical or sexual, or both, intimate partner violence against women in 2018.
entries.design: Systematic review + Bayesian multilevel modelling of prevalence data
entries.evidence_level: Systematic review with statistical modelling (global surveillance estimate)
entries.population_setting: 366 eligible studies, 2 million women, 161 countries/areas, ever-partnered women aged 15-49
entries.finding: Globally, 27% (UI 23-31%) of ever-partnered women aged 15-49 have experienced physical or sexual, or both, IPV in their lifetime, with 13% (10-16%) in the past year; violence starts early, affecting 24% (UI 21-28%) of women aged 15-19 and 26% (23-30%) aged 20-24.
entries.relevance_annotation: WHO/LSHTM global prevalence baseline underlying the burden argument for a marriage-transition governance threshold (P1); shows IPV risk is already established before/around the age most premarital couples marry, supporting the rationale for intervening at the marriage transition rather than proving T-PHE's effectiveness.
entries.verifier_note: 27% (UI 23-31%) lifetime and 13% (10-16%) past-year figures and the 24% (21-28%) for age 15-19 figure are verbatim-correct. But the record states '26% aged 20-24' while the fetched abstract literally reads '26% (23-30%) of women aged 19-24 years' (likely an upstream GBD/abstract typo, but the record must match the source text as fetched). FIX: change '20-24' to '19-24' to match the abstract exactly, or flag the age-band as ambiguous in a footnote.

entries.title: Findings from the SASA! Study: a cluster randomized controlled trial to assess the impact of a community mobilization intervention to prevent violence against women and reduce HIV risk in Kampala, Uganda.
entries.design: Pair-matched cluster randomized controlled trial (8 communities)
entries.population_setting: Community members aged 18-49, Kampala, Uganda; baseline n=1,583, follow-up n=2,532
entries.finding: SASA! was associated with significantly lower social acceptance of IPV among women (aRR 0.54, 95% CI 0.38-0.79) and 52% lower past-year physical IPV among women (0.48, 95% CI 0.16-1.39, crossing 1), plus higher likelihood of women receiving supportive community responses to disclosed violence.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P1/P2 (governance-layer, community-level mechanisms and visibility of concerns can shift norms and responses) but the physical-IPV effect's wide confidence interval crossing 1 is a caution relevant to T-PHE's own FAILURE CRITERION discipline about not over-claiming from attitudinal/knowledge shifts alone.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms aRR 0.54 (0.38-0.79) for lower acceptance of IPV among women, and 0.48 (0.16-1.39) for past-year physical IPV among women -- record correctly reports this CI crosses 1 and does not overclaim significance.

entries.first_author: Michau L / Kyegombe N (secondary mediation analysis of SASA! CRT)
entries.title: Ecological pathways to prevention: How does the SASA! community mobilisation model work to prevent physical intimate partner violence against women?
entries.design: Secondary mediation analysis of a cluster randomized controlled trial
entries.evidence_level: Mediation analysis nested in a cluster RCT
entries.population_setting: Community members aged 18-49, Kampala, Uganda (SASA! trial communities)
entries.finding: Community-level normative attitudes were the most important mediators of SASA!'s effect on physical IPV, explaining 70% of the effect on women's experience of IPV and 95% of the effect on men's perpetration; men's reduced suspicion of partner infidelity explained 22% of the effect on perpetration.
entries.relevance_annotation: Programme-theory/logic-model evidence that norms-change (not knowledge/attendance alone) is the operative mechanism for reducing IPV, directly supporting T-PHE's FAILURE CRITERION logic that knowledge/attendance/satisfaction rising without deeper mechanism change (informed choice, coercion recognition) would not constitute success.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms verbatim: community-level norms explained 70% of effect on women's IPV experience and 95% of effect on men's perpetration; men's reduced suspicion of infidelity explained 22% of perpetration effect.

entries.title: Cost and cost-effectiveness analysis of a community mobilisation intervention to reduce intimate partner violence in Kampala, Uganda.
entries.design: Economic evaluation alongside a cluster randomized controlled trial
entries.evidence_level: Economic evaluation nested in a cluster RCT
entries.population_setting: SASA! intervention communities, Kampala, Uganda, provider perspective, 4 years of programming
entries.finding: Total intervention cost over 4 years was estimated at US$553,252, averaging US$5 per person reached annually; an estimated 1,201 cases of past-year physical IPV were averted (90% CI 97-2,307) at a cost of US$460 per case averted.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant background for resourcing referral and safeguard infrastructure (P5, bounded authority and referral) in a conceptual synthesis that must reckon with feasibility of implementing multi-component safeguards, though it is a cost analysis of a different (community mobilization) programme model, not premarital education.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms US$553,252 total 4-year cost, US$5/person/year, 1,201 cases averted (90% CI 97-2,307), US$460/case averted -- all figures match exactly.

entries.title: SASA! Together: An evolution of the SASA! approach to prevent violence against women.
entries.design: Programme-theory/programme-description paper (non-empirical evaluation article)
entries.population_setting: Raising Voices programme learning, Uganda-originated model adapted for broader use
entries.finding: The paper describes the rationale for revising SASA! after ten years of programme learning and research, detailing how the revised 'SASA! Together' model incorporated field learning, and reflects on debates such as how best to scale up violence-prevention programmes.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly supports P7 (repairability) as a real-world precedent: an evidence-informed IPV-prevention programme explicitly built a formal revision cycle from accumulated field learning rather than treating its original design as fixed.
entries.verifier_note: Non-empirical programme-description paper confirmed; abstract supports the summary and the P7 (repairability) relevance framing (explicit revision cycle after 10 years of programme learning).

entries.title: Exploring Couples' Processes of Change in the Context of SASA!, a Violence Against Women and HIV Prevention Intervention in Uganda.
entries.design: Qualitative dyadic study (in-depth interviews, framework analysis)
entries.population_setting: Couples in SASA! intervention communities, Kampala, Uganda
entries.finding: Engagement with SASA! activities and relationship-skills/communication learning was associated with reduced conflict and IPV for many couples and increased trust, respect and joint economic problem-solving, though experiences and degree of change varied widely across couples.
entries.relevance_annotation: Illustrates a plausible mechanism for P1 (relationship-skills/communication content strengthening decision control and reducing conflict) but is drawn from ongoing established couples in a community-mobilisation context, not premarital screening; it does not test or validate T-PHE's STOP RULE logic that joint work must halt where coercive control is suspected, since this cohort was not selected for known violence risk.
entries.verifier_note: Key_finding content is supported by the abstract. However, first_author is wrong: the record lists 'Kyegombe N' but PubMed's actual first author for PMID 27682273 is 'Starmann E' (Kyegombe N appears to be a co-author, and is the correct first author on a different SASA! paper, PMID 30613427). FIX the first_author field to Starmann E before citing.

entries.title: Effective prevention of intimate partner violence through couples training: a randomised controlled trial of Indashyikirwa in Rwanda.
entries.design: Cluster randomized controlled trial (28 sectors)
entries.population_setting: Couples recruited from village savings and loan associations, rural Rwanda; 828 women/821 men intervention, 832 women/830 men control
entries.finding: At 24 months, women in intervention sectors were less likely to report physical/sexual IPV (aRR 0.44, 95% CI 0.34-0.59) and men less likely to report perpetration (aRR 0.54, 95% CI 0.38-0.75), with additional gains in acceptability of wife-beating, conflict management, communication, trust and self-efficacy, and no study-related harms detected.
entries.relevance_annotation: Strong supporting precedent for a structured couples-curriculum approach analogous to T-PHE: a couples-based curriculum plus community safeguards achieved a large, statistically robust reduction in IPV; the explicit 'no study-related harms' finding is relevant evidence that couples training, when structured, need not itself increase risk, but this trial screened via VSLA membership rather than a formal STOP RULE for suspected coercive control.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms aRR 0.44 (0.34-0.59) women, aRR 0.54 (0.38-0.75) men, and 'There were no study-related harms' verbatim.

entries.title: Shifting and transforming gender-inequitable beliefs, behaviours and norms in intimate partnerships: the Indashyikirwa couples' programme in Rwanda.
entries.design: Longitudinal qualitative study
entries.population_setting: Heterosexual couples participating in the Indashyikirwa curriculum, Rwanda
entries.finding: The curriculum, designed to build relationship skills and reduce gender-inequitable beliefs/behaviours/norms underpinning IPV, was associated with reported shifts in individual beliefs, couple relationship dynamics and gender norms among participating couples over time.
entries.relevance_annotation: Qualitative mechanism evidence supporting P1 (a structured relationship-skills curriculum can plausibly strengthen the individual/couple-level decision-control processes T-PHE targets), complementary to the Indashyikirwa RCT (PMID 33355268).
entries.verifier_note: Key_finding says the programme 'was associated with reported shifts...over time' but omits the abstract's explicit caveat that shifts were only 'moderate, but significant,' and that 'these shifts occurred without fully transforming deeply-entrenched beliefs and norms,' which the authors say could constrain longevity of change. Given T-PHE's own epistemic-humility/FAILURE CRITERION framing, this caveat should be added rather than presenting the finding as an unqualified positive shift.

entries.title: Lessons learned from implementing Indashyikirwa in Rwanda - an adaptation of the SASA! approach to prevent and respond to intimate partner violence.
entries.design: Implementation/adaptation review (qualitative evaluation and programme documentation)
entries.population_setting: Indashyikirwa programme, implemented by CARE Rwanda, RWAMREC and RWN, rural Rwanda
entries.finding: Indashyikirwa combined a 5-month couples curriculum, sustained community activism by trained couples, women's safe spaces for dedicated support and referral of IPV survivors, and training of opinion leaders to support an enabling environment; adaptation was guided by the SASA! fidelity brief.
entries.relevance_annotation: Close structural precedent for T-PHE's own multi-component safeguard architecture: it pairs a couples curriculum with a dedicated confidential referral pathway (women's safe spaces) and a defined enabling/authority structure, paralleling P4 (stop rule pending assessment), P5 (bounded authority and referral) and the affected-person-visibility safeguard.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms all four programme components (5-month couples curriculum, 2-year community activism, women's safe spaces, opinion-leader training) and the SASA! fidelity brief guidance verbatim.

entries.title: Shifting Norms in Faith Communities to Reduce Intimate Partner Violence: Results from a Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial of the Masculinity, Faith, and Peace Program in Nigeria.
entries.design: Two-arm, mixed-methods cluster randomized controlled trial (18-month faith-based, norms-shifting programme)
entries.population_setting: Women aged 18-35 (n=350) and male partners (n=281), from 10 Muslim and 10 Christian congregations, Plateau State, Nigeria
entries.finding: The Masculinity, Faith, and Peace (MFP) programme, delivered through faith congregations, assessed shifts in individual-, couple- and community-level social norms and IPV incidence in a mixed Muslim/Christian congregational sample; the trial was explicitly designed and powered to evaluate norms-shifting mechanisms rather than knowledge/attendance alone.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly relevant to P3 (cultural/religious tailoring, tested here across parallel Muslim and Christian congregations in one rigorous trial) and to the feasibility of delivering faith-based IPV-prevention content through religious leadership structures resembling T-PHE's premarital setting.
entries.verifier_note: Two problems. (1) key_finding omits the actual headline quantitative results reported in the abstract -- 'a significant 61% reduction in odds of reporting experiencing any IPV among women, a 64% reduction among Christians, and a 44% reduction in MFP congregations' -- and instead describes only the study design, which understates what was found; rewrite key_finding to include these effect sizes. The claim that the trial was 'explicitly designed and powered to evaluate norms-shifting mechanisms rather than knowledge/attendance alone' is not stated in the abstract and should be removed or re-sourced. (2) first_author is wrong: record lists 'Muluh N' but PubMed's actual first author is 'Shaw B'. FIX author field.

entries.title: Korean clergy for healthy families: online intervention for preventing intimate partner violence.
entries.design: Randomized controlled pilot trial (online modules, baseline and 3-month follow-up)
entries.population_setting: Korean American faith leaders, southeastern USA (n=55; intervention n=27, control n=28)
entries.finding: The intervention group showed significant improvement in knowledge of IPV resources and attitudes against IPV compared to control, but gains in self-efficacy and prevention/intervention behaviours, while greater than control, were not statistically significant.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly relevant to P5 (referral quality) since clergy are a plausible bounded-authority referral node, but the null result for self-efficacy/behaviour change is a cautionary complication for T-PHE's FAILURE CRITERION: raising knowledge/attitudes among gatekeepers does not guarantee improved safe help-seeking or accountable referral behaviour.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms significant improvement in knowledge/attitudes and a non-significant improvement in self-efficacy/behaviours verbatim.

entries.first_author: Le V (Archdiocese of Chicago Domestic Violence Outreach study)
entries.title: Qualitative Assessment of Key Implementation Factors in a Faith-Based Response to Intimate Partner Violence.
entries.design: Qualitative implementation study (16 semi-structured interviews, CFIR-coded)
entries.population_setting: Catholic diocesan and parish leadership, Archdiocese of Chicago Domestic Violence Outreach, USA
entries.finding: Using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, seven inner-setting constructs (leadership structure, culture, resources, networking/communication, access to knowledge, compatibility with parish values, leadership engagement) were identified as facilitators of successful diocesan-level IPV response implementation.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P5 (accountable referral requires organizational structure, not just goodwill) by showing that a faith institution's capacity to run an IPV response programme depends on defined leadership, resourcing and networked communication, structural preconditions T-PHE's bounded-authority safeguard would also need in a religious-organisation delivery setting.
entries.verifier_note: Key_finding content (seven CFIR inner-setting constructs and their content) is supported by the abstract. However, first_author is wrong: record lists 'Le V (Archdiocese of Chicago Domestic Violence Outreach study)' but PubMed's actual first author is 'Debinski B'. FIX the first_author field.

entries.title: Pathways of change: qualitative evaluations of intimate partner violence prevention programmes in Ghana, Rwanda, South Africa and Tajikistan.
entries.design: Comparative qualitative case study (secondary thematic analysis)
entries.population_setting: Participants across four IPV-prevention programmes, What Works to Prevent Violence against Women and Girls Programme (Ghana, Rwanda, South Africa, Tajikistan)
entries.finding: Similar cross-context pathways of change were identified: learning and applying relationship skills, participatory challenge of harmful gender norms with group rapport, and integration of economic-empowerment activities to reduce drivers of IPV and build self-confidence.
entries.relevance_annotation: Cross-context programme-theory evidence supporting P1 (relationship-skills content as a plausible mechanism for decision control) and P3 (participatory, culturally embedded delivery matters for whether norms-challenging content is accepted), useful for grounding T-PHE's programme theory in convergent findings across diverse settings rather than a single trial.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms the three cross-context pathways (relationship-skills learning, participatory norms-challenge, economic-empowerment integration) verbatim.

entries.title: Equipping community health workers in Rwanda to deliver a gender transformative parenting program to prevent violence.
entries.design: Pre/post training evaluation with phone follow-up
entries.population_setting: 573 community health workers, Burera district, Rwanda, delivering the Bandebereho programme at scale
entries.finding: Of 562 CHWs completing the pre-survey and 564 the post-survey (6-9 months later, plus 506 at 17-19 month follow-up), CHWs showed more equitable gender attitudes post-training; facilitators with more education showed smaller attitude shifts, underscoring the importance of sufficient time for facilitators' own transformation to maintain fidelity at scale.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant to bounded-authority/facilitator-competence safeguards: shows that scaling a violence-prevention curriculum through non-specialist community delivery agents (analogous to premarital course facilitators) requires structured, adequately dosed training to preserve fidelity, a caution for any scale-up of a T-PHE-style programme.
entries.verifier_note: Sample sizes (573 CHWs, 562/564 pre/post, 506 at 17-19mo follow-up) are verbatim-correct. But 'facilitators with more education showed smaller attitude shifts' misstates the abstract: the regression finding is that CHWs with some secondary education (coef -2.15, p<0.01) and >3 years' experience (coef -2.27, p<0.001) were LESS LIKELY to hold inequitable attitudes -- a baseline/associational finding about attitude levels, not a finding about the SIZE of pre/post attitude shift during training. Reword key_finding to avoid implying a dose-response on 'shift magnitude' that the abstract does not report.

entries.title: Effectiveness of the Moments that Matter parenting programme on caregiving practices, family violence, mental health and other outcomes: a cluster-randomised controlled trial in Kenya.
entries.design: Cluster randomized controlled trial
entries.population_setting: 595 caregiver-child dyads (children aged 0-18 months) in 46 villages, western Kenya, delivered via community volunteers partnered with faith leaders
entries.finding: At endline there were no overall intervention effects on the primary outcome (child development), though moderate-to-large effects were observed on several secondary outcomes including caregiver stimulation, harsh discipline, caregiver mental health, social support, and intimate partner violence victimisation as reported by female caregivers.
entries.relevance_annotation: A directly cautionary case for T-PHE's FAILURE CRITERION: a rigorously trialled, faith-leader-partnered community programme showed a null result on its declared primary outcome while showing improvement on secondary/downstream outcomes (including IPV victimisation), illustrating exactly the kind of outcome-selection pitfall T-PHE's failure criterion is designed to guard against (do not let secondary or proxy gains substitute for the declared primary target).
entries.verifier_note: Key_finding content (null primary child-development outcome, moderate-to-large secondary effects including IPV victimisation) is well supported and the FAILURE CRITERION framing in relevance_to_tphe is apt. However, first_author is a placeholder '(MTM Kenya trial investigators)' rather than PubMed's actual first author 'Jeong J'. FIX the first_author field.

entries.title: Community based intervention to prevent domestic violence against women in the reproductive age in Northwestern Ethiopia: a study protocol for community based cluster randomized trial.
entries.design: Study protocol for a community-based quasi-experimental/cluster trial
entries.population_setting: 1,269 women planned across intervention, active comparator and control groups, Awi zone, northwestern Ethiopia
entries.finding: The protocol describes a planned pilot of translating existing evidence and policy into community-level domestic-violence prevention via peer education, community representative training, husband involvement and integration with community health extension programmes; no outcome data are reported (protocol only).
entries.relevance_annotation: Illustrates the broader field's emphasis on husband/partner involvement and community health-worker integration as delivery channels for IPV prevention (echoing P1's governance-layer logic), but as a protocol paper it provides no outcome evidence and should not be cited for effectiveness.
entries.verifier_note: Confirmed as a study protocol with no outcome data (no Results section in the abstract); record correctly flags 'should not be cited for effectiveness'.

entries.title: Community activism as a strategy to reduce intimate partner violence (IPV) in rural Rwanda: Results of a community randomised trial.
entries.design: Cluster randomized controlled trial (community-level activism component)
entries.population_setting: Rural Rwanda, adaptation of the SASA! community-activism model
entries.finding: There was no evidence of an intervention effect on any primary or secondary trial outcome, including women's past-year experience of physical and/or sexual IPV from a current partner (adjusted odds ratio 1.25, 95% CI 0.92-1.70), i.e. a null/non-significant result in the direction of possible harm.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly complicates any assumption that community-mobilisation or norms-based prevention strategies reliably reduce IPV: a rigorous RCT of an adapted, well-regarded model found no protective effect, reinforcing the need for T-PHE's own FAILURE CRITERION and epistemic-humility safeguard rather than assuming a plausible-sounding mechanism will translate into real protection.
entries.verifier_note: Null-result key_finding (aOR 1.25, 95% CI 0.92-1.70) is verbatim-correct and appropriately characterized as null/non-significant. However, first_author is wrong: record lists 'Dunkle K' but PubMed's actual first author for PMID 32257154 is 'Chatterji S' (Dunkle K is the correct first author for the different Indashyikirwa RCT paper, PMID 33355268 -- the two appear to have been conflated). FIX the first_author field.

entries.title: Changing the norms that drive intimate partner violence: findings from a cluster randomised trial on what predisposes bystanders to intervene.
entries.design: Cross-sectional survey nested within a cluster randomised trial (SASA! study)
entries.evidence_level: Cross-sectional survey nested in a cluster RCT
entries.population_setting: Community members aged 18-49 who had witnessed IPV, Kampala, Uganda, 4 years post-intervention
entries.finding: SASA! community members who had witnessed IPV were substantially more likely to try to help than control-community counterparts (57% vs 31%); associated factors differed by trial arm, with SASA!-community bystander action linked to relationship duration, employment, talking to neighbours and SASA! exposure.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P2 (a norms-shifted community/social environment increases visibility of, and willingness to respond to, concerns about violence), relevant background for why T-PHE frames private-channel and community-facing safeguards as complementary rather than substitutable.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 57% vs 31% bystander intervention rate verbatim, and the listed associated factors are a fair subset of the abstract's fuller list.

entries.title: Adapting, Sustaining and Scaling Violence against Women and Children Prevention Interventions in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Scoping Review of Implementation Science Approaches.
entries.design: Scoping review
entries.population_setting: 40 VAW/C evaluation studies with implementation or process-evaluation components (2023-2024 review period), low- and middle-income country focus
entries.finding: Commonly used implementation frameworks were CFIR, EPIS and MRC frameworks, with fidelity, acceptability and feasibility most studied; scale and sustainability, and survivor-centred practice/practice-based knowledge, were only minimally addressed in the reviewed literature.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly relevant to T-PHE's status as a programme-theory/logic-model synthesis: confirms that formal implementation-science framing (which T-PHE's six safeguards and stop rule resemble) is under-used in VAW/C prevention research and that scale/sustainability and survivor-centredness remain evidence gaps, supporting T-PHE's own epistemic-humility framing rather than a claim of proven effectiveness.
entries.verifier_note: Key_finding content (CFIR/EPIS/MRC frameworks; fidelity/acceptability/feasibility most studied; scale/sustainability and survivor-centred practice under-addressed) matches the abstract. However, first_author is a placeholder '(VAW/C implementation science scoping review authors)' rather than PubMed's actual first author 'Falb KL'. FIX the first_author field.

entries.title: Does marriage and relationship education work? A meta-analytic study.
entries.journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
entries.design: Meta-analysis (86 reports, 117 studies, >500 effect sizes)
entries.evidence_level: Meta-analysis of RCTs/quasi-experiments (high on communication/satisfaction outcomes; silent on safety outcomes)
entries.population_setting: Mostly US/Western MRE program participants; predominantly White, middle-class samples
entries.finding: Relationship-quality effect sizes for experimental studies ranged d=.30-.36 and communication-skills effects d=.43-.45; moderate-dosage programs outperformed low-dosage; the authors flag that racial/ethnic and economic diversity was too thin to draw reliable conclusions for disadvantaged couples, and that outcomes policymakers care about (relationship stability, aggression) were rarely measured.
entries.relevance_annotation: Foundational MRE effectiveness base rate. Directly relevant to the FAILURE CRITERION: shows conventional MRE literature has historically measured satisfaction/communication, not coercion recognition or safe help-seeking -- supports T-PHE's premise that a governance/decision-control layer measures something existing MRE evidence has not captured (complicates P1/P6 by showing the evidence gap T-PHE claims to address is real).
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms all numeric claims verbatim: 'The effect sizes for relationship quality for experimental studies ranged from d = .30 to .36, while the communication skills effect sizes ranged from d = .43 to .45. ... Moderate-dosage programs produced larger effect sizes than did low-dosage programs.' Diversity/policy-outcome gap directly quoted: 'a lack of racial/ethnic and economic diversity in the samples prevented reliable conclusions about the effectiveness of MRE for disadvantaged couples ... intervention outcomes important to policy makers, such as relationship stability and aggression, rarely have been addressed.' Relevance claim (evidence gap re: safety/coercion outcomes) is accurate, not overstated.

entries.title: Exploring programmatic moderators of the effectiveness of marriage and relationship education programs: a meta-analytic study.
entries.design: Meta-analysis (148 evaluation reports)
entries.population_setting: Mixed university/laboratory and religious-setting MRE programs, largely US
entries.finding: Moderate-dosage programs (9-20 contact hours) had stronger effects than low-dosage (1-8 hours); a communication-skills emphasis strengthened communication outcomes but not satisfaction; no evidence that formal institutionalization (manuals, trainer certification) improved effects, and no significant difference between religious-setting and university/laboratory delivery.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant to P1 (governance layer vs. content dose) and the religious-setting question directly germane to a TIMA/FIMA programme: dosage/format moderators mattered more than institutional formality or religious vs secular venue in this meta-analytic evidence -- neither strongly supports nor refutes a specific governance-layer effect, since no P1-type 'decision-control' variable was ever coded.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'moderate-dosage programs (9-20 contact hours) were associated with stronger effects compared to low-dosage programs (1-8 contact hours)... A programmatic emphasis on communication skills was associated with stronger effects on couple communication outcomes, but this difference did not reach statistical significance for the relationship quality/satisfaction outcome... no evidence that institutionalized MRE programs... were associated with stronger effects. Similarly, there was little evidence of differences in program setting (university/laboratory vs. religious).' Matches record exactly. Relevance claim correctly notes no P1-type decision-control variable was coded (honest, not overstated).

entries.title: How effective are ACF-funded couple relationship education programs? A meta-analytic study.
entries.design: Meta-analysis (32 control-group studies + 19 one-group pre-post studies)
entries.population_setting: US lower-income couples/individuals enrolled in federally funded (ACF Healthy Marriage and Relationship Education) CRE programs
entries.finding: Small but significant effects for relationship quality (d=.114), relationship skills (d=.132), mental health (d=.074) and coparenting (d=.033); effects on relationship stability, parenting and child well-being were non-significant.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly supports the FAILURE CRITERION logic: a large, well-funded government MRE effort shows small quality/skills gains but null effects on stability -- exactly the kind of pattern (soft-outcome movement without the harder outcome) T-PHE's failure criterion is designed to catch if applied to decision-control/coercion-recognition outcomes instead.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'a range of small but significant effects for couple relationship quality (d = .114), relationship skills (d = .132), mental health (d = .074), and coparenting (d = .033), but non-significant effects for relationship stability, parenting, and child well-being.' All d-values and null-on-stability finding match exactly. Relevance claim (small quality gains without stability gains as a template for a possible coercion-outcome failure pattern) is a reasonable analogy, clearly framed as illustrative not as direct evidence about coercion outcomes.

entries.title: A randomized clinical trial of the effectiveness of premarital intervention: moderators of divorce outcomes.
entries.design: Randomized controlled trial (couples via religious organizations randomized to PREP vs. naturally occurring premarital services; n=44/66/83)
entries.population_setting: US couples marrying through religious organizations, 8-year follow-up on divorce
entries.finding: No overall difference in divorce rates between PREP (clergy-delivered or professional-delivered) and usual premarital services; couples with higher premarital negative-communication observed pre-intervention were MORE likely to divorce if given PREP, while low-negativity couples benefited; a premarital history of physical aggression showed a similar (marginally significant) harmful-moderation pattern.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates and partially supports T-PHE. It is a key evidence source for the STOP RULE / P4 logic: standard joint-couple relationship education can worsen outcomes for couples with pre-existing negative communication or aggression -- exactly the population the STOP RULE and coercion-screening safeguard are meant to route away from ordinary joint education. Also complicates P1/failure criterion: a rigorously delivered, faith-setting RCT of premarital education found no divorce-rate benefit overall, i.e. conventional-outcome success is not guaranteed even with religious-organization delivery.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'no differences in overall divorce rates between naturally occurring services... PREP delivered by clergy... or PREP delivered by professionals'; 'couples observed to have higher levels of negative communication in a video task were more likely to divorce if they received PREP than if they received naturally occurring services'; 'A history of physical aggression... showed a similar pattern as a moderator, but the effect was only marginally significant.' All matches. This is the strongest, most literal PubMed evidence for the STOP RULE (P4) logic in the whole record set.

entries.title: Risk moderates the outcome of relationship education: a randomized controlled trial.
entries.journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
entries.design: RCT (N=130 engaged/newlywed couples randomized to 1 of 3 relationship-education programs, 3-year follow-up)
entries.population_setting: US engaged and newlywed couples
entries.finding: Couples with acute baseline concerns, including higher physical aggression and alcohol use, benefited LESS from relationship-education intervention than couples without these concerns; couples with high baseline satisfaction/commitment actually declined faster in satisfaction under an intensive skill-based intervention versus a low-intensity one.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly supports the STOP RULE (P4) and bounded-authority safeguard: this RCT is empirical evidence that undifferentiated relationship-skills intervention is not uniformly beneficial and can be counterproductive for higher-risk couples (aggression, substance use), reinforcing the case for a screening/stop mechanism before joint work rather than one-size-fits-all joint education.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'Couples with acute concerns at baseline, including higher levels of physical aggression and alcohol use, benefitted less from intervention than couples without these concerns... couples with relatively high baseline satisfaction and commitment scores declined faster in satisfaction when assigned to an intensive skill-based intervention.' Matches record. Correctly cited as direct RCT support for a stop/screen mechanism (P4).

entries.title: Does premarital education decrease or increase couples' later help-seeking?
entries.design: Cross-sectional survey study (N=2,126 married individuals)
entries.evidence_level: Cross-sectional survey, self-report; associative not causal
entries.population_setting: US married adults, general population sample
entries.finding: Contrary to the assumption that premarital education reduces later need for counseling, receiving premarital education covaried with an INCREASED likelihood of later couples counseling (a 'gateway' effect), with the association stronger among African Americans and those with lower income/education.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly relevant to P2 (private channel making concerns visible) and the safe help-seeking outcome domain in the FAILURE CRITERION: empirical evidence that premarital education can function as a gateway that increases later formal help-seeking rather than substituting for it -- supports the plausibility that a T-PHE-style programme could raise help-seeking as an intended (not a failure) outcome, and is directly usable evidence for the referral-quality proposition (P5).
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'Consistent with the gateway hypothesis, receiving premarital education covaried with an increased likelihood of receiving couples counseling. The association... was moderated by demographic indicators, with the association being stronger for African Americans and for individuals with lower incomes and less formal education.' Matches record. Relevance claim to P2/P5 correctly labeled 'associative not causal' in evidence_level field, appropriately hedged.

entries.title: Barriers and facilitators of relationship help-seeking among low-income couples.
entries.design: Cross-sectional self-report study (N=231 ethnically diverse newlywed couples in low-income neighborhoods)
entries.population_setting: US low-income newlywed couples
entries.finding: Top perceived barriers to seeking couple therapy were cost and uncertainty about where to go for help; direct experience with premarital education (or indirect experience via a social-network member's couple therapy) was associated with reduced barriers and greater likelihood of subsequently seeking therapy.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P2/P5 (private-channel visibility, referral quality = timeliness + accessibility + follow-through): identifies 'not knowing where to go' as a leading real-world barrier, which is precisely what an accountable-referral safeguard is designed to close; usable evidence base for why referral pathway design matters independent of content quality.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'men and women identify cost and uncertainty about where to go for help as their top two barriers to seeking therapy for the relationship... Direct and indirect experiences with relationship interventions was associated with increased likelihood that couples sought therapy.' Matches record. Relevance to referral-quality proposition (P5) is reasonable — the finding is specifically about pathway/accessibility barriers, not content quality, so it legitimately supports P5 rather than being stretched to a safety claim.

entries.title: The role of leaders' working alliance in premarital education.
entries.design: RCT sub-analysis (31 leaders training 118 couples/236 attendees in a PREP trial)
entries.population_setting: US couples in a randomized PREP trial, multiple facilitators
entries.finding: Relationship outcomes varied significantly by which leader delivered the training; facilitators' aggregated working-alliance quality (as rated by attendees) predicted change in observed communication and relationship satisfaction, over and above curriculum content itself.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant to dignity-and-consent and cultural-intelligibility safeguards and to P3: shows facilitator relational quality, not just curriculum content, drives outcomes -- supports the T-PHE premise that governance/process factors (who delivers, how) matter as much as content, and is a caution that programme fidelity depends on facilitator training/alliance, which T-PHE would need to operationalize for its own safeguards to be more than aspirational.
entries.verifier_note: Core numeric/qualitative claims are supported: 'couples' relationship outcomes from pre- to post-training varied on the basis of the leader'; 'Leaders' aggregated working alliance quality also explained change in relationship satisfaction.' However the record's phrase 'over and above curriculum content itself' is an inference, not a direct quote — the abstract shows alliance and PREP-training both independently explaining variability but never states alliance effects held net of controlling for content/curriculum in a formal sense. FIX: soften key_finding to 'predicted change... alongside curriculum/training condition' rather than 'over and above curriculum content itself,' since the abstract does not report a controlled comparison isolating alliance from content.

entries.title: Revising Premarital Relationship Interventions for the Next Generation.
entries.journal: Journal of Marital and Family Therapy
entries.design: Narrative review/position paper
entries.evidence_level: Narrative review / expert opinion (no primary data)
entries.population_setting: General discussion of contemporary premarital-education practice, US-centric
entries.finding: Reviews social trends (individualism/commitment ambivalence, changing marriage attitudes, premarital relationship histories, media environment) and argues current premarital interventions need updated content and structure to remain relevant to engaged couples today; offers four proposals for redesigning premarital interventions.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports the conceptual-synthesis framing of T-PHE itself (P1, P7): an independent call from within the MRE field for programme redesign and modernization, i.e., precedent for treating premarital education as needing structural/governance revision rather than only content updates -- but is itself non-empirical (opinion/review), so provides conceptual not evidentiary support.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'we examine four general, interrelated social trends: individualism and commitment ambivalence, changing attitudes about marriage, premarital relationship histories, and the omnipresent media environment... we offer four general proposals.' Matches record's description as a narrative/position paper. Correctly labeled non-empirical, conceptual support only.

entries.title: Can marriage education mitigate the risks associated with premarital cohabitation?
entries.design: RCT / secondary analysis (PREP for married couples in the U.S. Army, N=662 couples)
entries.evidence_level: RCT / secondary analysis of trial data
entries.population_setting: US Army married couples
entries.finding: Precommitment cohabitation (cohabiting before a mutual commitment to marry) was associated with lower marital satisfaction/dedication and higher divorce by 2-year follow-up in the control group, but this risk was NOT apparent in the PREP intervention group -- i.e., the education program appeared to buffer a known risk factor.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates the FAILURE CRITERION in a useful way: this is exactly the kind of study T-PHE would need to be cautious about generalizing from -- it shows conventional relationship-education content CAN buffer a specific relational risk factor (cohabitation-associated distress) on conventional outcomes (satisfaction, divorce), which supports the plausibility that content-only programmes have real protective value, a nuance T-PHE's framework should not erase even while insisting content alone is insufficient for coercion/safety outcomes.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'significant interactions between intervention condition and cohabitation history indicated that for the control group, but not the PREP group, precommitment cohabitation was associated with lower dedication as well as declines in marital satisfaction... those with precommitment cohabitation were more likely to divorce by the 2-year follow-up only in the control group.' Matches record precisely (buffering effect). Relevance claim is candid that this complicates rather than simply supports T-PHE — appropriate framing, not overstated.

entries.title: 10-Year Study of Christian Church Support for Domestic Violence Victims: 2005-2015.
entries.design: Repeated cross-sectional survey (convenience sample of Upper-Midwest US congregations, 2005 and 2015)
entries.population_setting: Christian clergy and congregation members, US
entries.finding: Faith commitments led some domestic-violence victims to endure abuse rather than compromise their faith by leaving; over 10 years, congregational support for victims changed slowly; clergy wanted more training in counseling and speaking about domestic violence, and felt comfortable making referrals but not necessarily providing direct DV counseling themselves.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly supports the STOP RULE and bounded-authority-and-referral safeguard (P4/P5): faith-based settings can inadvertently keep victims in danger when religious framing discourages leaving, and clergy themselves report needing referral pathways rather than attempting DV counseling directly -- strong real-world grounding for why joint faith-based marriage-preparation work must stop and refer, not proceed, when coercion/violence is suspected.
entries.verifier_note: Key_finding is well supported: 'Victims find strength in their faith and would rather endure the violence at all costs to keep a family or a marriage together, than to compromise their faith by leaving' and 'Clergy felt comfortable in making referrals for professional counseling.' However relevance_to_tphe overstates the referral point: the abstract's very next clause is 'while the majority of members would prefer counseling with their pastor if they were in a violent relationship' — i.e. congregants actually want direct pastoral counseling, not referral, and clergy said they want MORE training to counsel/speak about DV themselves, not that they prefer referral over direct counseling. FIX: change 'clergy themselves report needing referral pathways rather than attempting DV counseling directly' to something like 'clergy report comfort in making referrals, while members/clergy simultaneously want more direct pastoral counseling capacity — a live tension rather than clean support for a refer-not-counsel policy that T-PHE's safeguard should note, not paper over.'

entries.title: Culturally specific treatment for partner-abusive Latino men: a qualitative study to identify and implement program components.
entries.design: Qualitative study (demographic survey + qualitative interviews) informing program design
entries.evidence_level: Qualitative study (program-development evidence, not outcome trial)
entries.population_setting: Latino immigrant men who are intimate-partner-violence perpetrators, Southern California
entries.finding: A culturally specific, Spanish-language program integrating gender roles, immigration/discrimination context, marital sexual abuse, and spirituality was seen by participants as more relevant; the study explicitly frames cultural sensitivity as compatible with, not a substitute for, perpetrator accountability.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant to P3 (cultural tailoring helps only if it does not override consent/safety): this is evidence for the general design principle that culturally specific adaptation of violence-related intervention content is feasible and valued by participants WITHOUT diminishing accountability -- supports the T-PHE claim that cultural intelligibility and non-negotiable safety/accountability can coexist, though this study concerns perpetrator treatment, not premarital education, so applicability to T-PHE's couple-education context is indirect.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'Results suggest the desirability of an empathic and culturally-sensitive approach, without diminishing responsibility.' Matches 'compatible with, not a substitute for, perpetrator accountability.' Relevance claim correctly flags this concerns perpetrator treatment, not premarital couple education — applicability to T-PHE explicitly marked indirect, appropriately hedged.

entries.title: Prevention of marital dysfunction: behavioral approaches and beyond.
entries.design: Narrative review of 13 program-evaluation studies
entries.population_setting: General review of behaviorally oriented marriage-preparation programs, mostly US
entries.finding: Behaviorally oriented, skills-based marriage-preparation programs across 13 reviewed studies showed evidence of producing behavioral changes that may help prevent marital dysfunction, though program-evaluation methodology at the time was described as only modestly improved and needing further rigor.
entries.relevance_annotation: Historical evidence base for P6 (conventional success can coexist with failure): an early review already flagged methodological weakness in outcome measurement for marriage-preparation programs, i.e., the evidentiary gap T-PHE's failure criterion targets (measuring only satisfaction/skills, not coercion-recognition/safety) has been a recognized limitation in the field for decades, not a new critique invented by T-PHE.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'The results of 13 studies suggest that behaviorally oriented, skills-based marriage preparation programs can lead to behavioral changes that may help prevent the emergence of marital dysfunction. Whereas there has been modest improvement in the methodology of the program evaluations, suggestions for continued improvements are made.' Matches record. Relevance claim (methodological weakness as a decades-old recognized limitation) is directly supported.

entries.title: Improving practice in marriage preparation.
entries.design: Narrative review
entries.evidence_level: Narrative review / practice guidance (no primary outcome data)
entries.population_setting: General review of marriage-preparation program practice, US
entries.finding: Reviews two decades of research on marriage-preparation programs and gives design recommendations covering needs assessment, timing/duration, format, content, provider characteristics, and promotion; does not report new outcome data.
entries.relevance_annotation: Background/context support for P7 (repairability) and overall programme-design literature: establishes needs assessment and provider characteristics as long-recognized levers for programme quality, consistent with T-PHE's emphasis on governance and safeguard design rather than content alone, but is descriptive/prescriptive, not an outcome evaluation.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms this is a review with 'Issues reviewed include assessing client needs, the timing and duration of programs, formats and methods, program content, provider characteristics, and promotion and marketing strategies' and no primary outcome data. Matches record and correctly labeled descriptive/prescriptive, not evaluative.

entries.title: Changes in premarital counseling as related to older cohorts of married couples.
entries.design: Retrospective cohort survey (N=256 current/former members of a Christian denomination)
entries.population_setting: Members of the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), US
entries.finding: Over successive marriage cohorts, premarital counseling availability, voluntariness, and duration increased, but self-reported effectiveness of premarital counseling did not significantly change across cohorts -- possibly because marital challenges grew in complexity at a comparable rate.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports the FAILURE CRITERION logic historically: increased 'dose' and formalization of faith-based premarital counseling over time did not translate into perceived improvement in effectiveness, an early empirical parallel to T-PHE's claim that conventional programme growth (attendance, hours) can occur without improvement on the outcomes that matter.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'the reported effectiveness of their premarital counseling experience was not significantly related to years since marriage. It is possible that even though the quality of premarital counseling may have improved over time, the challenges and complexity of marriage may have changed at a similar rate, resulting in no net change.' Matches record's paraphrase closely. Relevance claim (dose/formalization increase without perceived-effectiveness gain) is directly supported and not overstated.

entries.title: Videoconferencing Delivery of the Seoul Premarital Education Program During COVID-19: A Quasi-experimental Study Using Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting.
entries.design: Quasi-experimental study with inverse probability of treatment weighting (weighted N=291 women, 228 men)
entries.population_setting: Couples in a city-wide (Seoul) premarital education program, South Korea, during COVID-19
entries.finding: Videoconferencing delivery of the Seoul Premarital Education Program (S-PEP) was associated with increased marital readiness for both men and women, and with increased relationship confidence and satisfaction for women specifically.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant background for delivery-format questions (not directly Muslim/Thai context, but a non-Western, government-run premarital program) and for P1: like the ACF and Hawkins meta-analyses, measures only readiness/confidence/satisfaction, not decision control, coercion recognition, or safe help-seeking -- again illustrating the FAILURE CRITERION's evidentiary gap rather than contradicting T-PHE.
entries.verifier_note: Key_finding matches: 'S-PEP via VC was effective in increasing levels of marital readiness for both women and men and in enhancing relationship confidence and satisfaction for women.' Year check: PubMed's JournalIssue citation year is 2026 (Prevention Science assigned this to a 2026 issue), but the article's actual electronic publication / PubMed indexing date is 2025-01-06 and the study itself was conducted during 'the early COVID-19 period' (i.e. ~2020-2021 data). This is a legitimate ahead-of-print/issue-year artifact, not an error, but FIX: add a one-line caveat in the record noting the 2026 tag is the journal's assigned print-issue year, not the study's data-collection period, so a reader doesn't assume this is a 2026 study of a 2026 phenomenon.

entries.title: Premarital intervention based on attachment and differentiation improves communication and conflict management in Iranian couples.
entries.design: Quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control-group study (N=40, 20 couples: 10 experimental, 10 control)
entries.population_setting: Engaged couples at a university-affiliated counseling center, Iran (collectivist-society context)
entries.finding: An 8-10 session attachment/differentiation-based premarital intervention produced significant post-intervention improvements in integrating, obliging and compromising communication styles and reduced avoidance/dominating styles (MANCOVA F=8.73-42.16, p<.01-.001) versus no-treatment control.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant comparator from a Muslim-majority, collectivist-culture setting close to T-PHE's own context: demonstrates conventional communication/conflict-skills gains are achievable in a culturally analogous population, again on process outcomes (communication style) rather than decision-control, coercion-recognition, or safe help-seeking -- useful as a 'what conventional success looks like' contrast case for the FAILURE CRITERION, and note the very small sample (n=20 couples) limits generalizability.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract F-statistics: integrating F=21.90, obliging F=19.49, compromising F=8.73, dominating F=9.53 (reduced), avoidance F=42.16 (reduced) — record's summarized range 'F=8.73-42.16, p<.01-.001' correctly spans the reported values. Session count '8-10 structured ADPM-based sessions' matches. N=40 (20 couples: 10/10) matches. Relevance claim correctly flags the small sample (n=20 couples) as a generalizability limit.

entries.title: Cultural adaptation and pilot evaluation of the Couple Learning Program (CLP) among young Turkish couples: A mixed-method study.
entries.design: Pilot randomized controlled trial, mixed methods (N=8 couples primary phase + 2 couples feasibility phase)
entries.evidence_level: Pilot RCT, very small sample (feasibility-level evidence)
entries.population_setting: Young premarital couples, Turkey (culturally adapted European program)
entries.finding: A culturally adapted, 6-session Couple Learning Program produced significant improvements in conflict-resolution strategies (exit, voice, neglect dimensions) with relationship satisfaction improving only at follow-up (not immediately post-intervention); participants rated the culturally adapted program as relevant and acceptable.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly relevant to P3 (cultural tailoring helps only if culture does not override consent/safety): a rare pilot RCT of a Western-origin couple program culturally adapted for a Muslim-majority country, demonstrating feasibility and acceptability of cultural adaptation -- supports P3's premise that tailoring can improve engagement, though the extremely small pilot sample (8 couples) means this is preliminary feasibility evidence, not a powered effectiveness trial, and it still measures only communication/satisfaction, not safety or decision-control outcomes.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'significant improvements in conflict resolution strategies-particularly in exit, voice, and neglect dimensions-while no significant change was observed in the loyalty response... a significant increase in relationship satisfaction emerged only at the follow-up stage... involved eight couples' plus a separate two-couple feasibility phase. Matches record's N breakdown and satisfaction-only-at-follow-up detail precisely. Relevance claim correctly labels this preliminary feasibility evidence, not a powered trial.

entries.title: Perceived need of information and education about conception preparedness (CP) among engaged and soon to be married couples: a qualitative survey.
entries.design: Qualitative descriptive study (focus group discussions, N=40 engaged couples)
entries.population_setting: Engaged couples recruited at premarital counseling sites (churches, sector administration offices), Rwanda
entries.finding: Engaged couples identified specific unmet information/education needs regarding conception preparedness, with premarital counseling sites (including religious venues) identified as a natural point of contact; themes included knowledge gaps, motivators for seeking information, and desired educational content.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports the needs-assessment/participant-voice premise underlying affected-person visibility (safeguard) and P2: independent qualitative evidence that couples at premarital counseling touchpoints (including faith-based sites) have specific, articulable information needs beyond what standard premarital counseling covers -- reinforces the case for content and process gaps that a governance-aware programme could address, though this study concerns reproductive/conception content specifically, not decision-control or coercion recognition.
entries.verifier_note: Key_finding themes are supported: abstract lists 'knowledge and understanding, motivators for seeking information, desired educational content, preferred information sources, and urgency of education' as the five themes, and record's subset (knowledge gaps, motivators, desired content) is accurate. However relevance_to_tphe claim that 'premarital counseling sites ... identified as a natural point of contact' overstates the abstract: churches/sector offices were the STUDY's recruitment sites (where couples were sampled), not a finding that participants themselves nominated those sites as their preferred point of contact — the abstract instead reports 'Health professionals were the preferred information source, with schools, churches, and social media also mentioned,' i.e. churches were a secondary preference behind health professionals. FIX: rewrite the relevance claim to say premarital counseling venues were used as the recruitment/sampling frame in this study and were only a secondary (not primary) preferred information source per participants, so the 'natural point of contact' framing should be removed or clearly attributed to study design rather than participant preference.

entries.title: Effect of Premarital Education on the Quality of Life of Female Partners: A Cross-Sectional Study.
entries.design: Cross-sectional study (N=596 Saudi women married <=15 years)
entries.evidence_level: Cross-sectional survey; associative, self-report, no control group
entries.population_setting: Saudi women, general population, Muslim-majority context
entries.finding: Only 37.2% of participants had received premarital counseling/education, although 86.4% believed it was crucial before marriage; women who received premarital education/counseling and rated it as impactful had significantly higher WHOQOL-BREF quality-of-life scores.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly relevant background evidence for a Muslim-majority premarital-education context (though Saudi rather than Thai): documents a large gap between perceived importance (86.4%) and actual uptake (37.2%) of premarital education, supporting the rationale for scaling programmes like T-PHE in comparable settings; however, the cross-sectional, self-selected design cannot establish that education caused the quality-of-life association, and the outcome measured is general quality of life, not decision control, coercion recognition, or safe help-seeking -- illustrates the FAILURE CRITERION gap again (a positive conventional-outcome association says nothing about the governance-specific outcomes T-PHE targets).
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'Only 37.2% of the participants had premarital counseling and education, even though 86.4% thought it was crucial before marriage... The mean WHOQOL-BREF score... was considerably higher for participants who indicated that premarital education significantly impacted the quality of their marriage and those who received premarital counseling.' Matches record's percentages and QoL association. Relevance claim correctly caveats this as cross-sectional/associative with no control group and explicitly notes it says nothing about decision-control or coercion-recognition outcomes — appropriately hedged, not overstated.

entries.title: Screening for Intimate Partner Violence and Caregiver Abuse of Older or Vulnerable Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
entries.design: guideline / recommendation statement (systematic-review-based)
entries.population_setting: US adolescents and adults, pregnant/postpartum and reproductive-age women; older/vulnerable adults without recognized signs of abuse
entries.finding: USPSTF concludes screening for IPV in women of reproductive age (including pregnant/postpartum), combined with provision or referral to multicomponent interventions, has moderate net benefit (B recommendation). For caregiver abuse/neglect of older or vulnerable adults, benefits and harms remain undetermined (I statement) even in this 2025 update.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly supports P5 (referral quality: timeliness, accessibility, follow-through) and the FAILURE CRITERION logic -- the global-guidance benefit is conditional on referral/intervention, not screening/knowledge alone; the persistent I-statement for vulnerable-adult abuse also cautions against assuming any T-PHE mechanism 'works' in undertested subpopulations.
entries.verifier_note: Title, year (2025), journal (JAMA) all match. Abstract confirms exactly: 'screening for IPV in women of reproductive age...and providing or referring those who screen positive to multicomponent interventions has a moderate net benefit...(B recommendation)' and 'benefits and harms of screening for caregiver abuse and neglect in older or vulnerable adults are uncertain...(I statement).' relevance_to_tphe is reasonable and not overstated.

entries.title: Screening for Intimate Partner Violence, Elder Abuse, and Abuse of Vulnerable Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Final Recommendation Statement
entries.design: guideline / recommendation statement
entries.evidence_level: Global guidance (USPSTF recommendation statement, moderate-certainty evidence)
entries.population_setting: US women of reproductive age; older/vulnerable adults
entries.finding: With moderate certainty, screening plus referral to ongoing support services has moderate net benefit; explicitly states evidence does NOT support the effectiveness of brief interventions or merely providing referral information in the absence of ongoing supportive intervention components, and that benefit evidence is concentrated in pregnant/postpartum populations.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly complicates P5/referral-quality claims and the STOP RULE's assumption that referral alone suffices -- explicit global-guidance evidence that a referral pamphlet/information-only pathway is not established as effective; supports the T-PHE emphasis on accountable, ongoing referral rather than a one-time hand-off.
entries.verifier_note: Confirmed by abstract: 'moderate net benefit...The evidence does not support the effectiveness of brief interventions or the provision of information about referral options in the absence of ongoing supportive intervention components. The evidence demonstrating benefit of ongoing support services is predominantly found in studies of pregnant or postpartum women.' Matches key_finding closely.

entries.title: Screening for intimate partner violence and abuse of elderly and vulnerable adults: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendation statement
entries.design: guideline / recommendation statement
entries.population_setting: US asymptomatic women of reproductive age; elderly and vulnerable adults
entries.finding: First USPSTF B-grade recommendation to screen women of childbearing age for IPV and refer positive screens to intervention services, updating a 2004 insufficient-evidence (I) statement; evidence for elderly/vulnerable-adult screening remained insufficient (I statement).
entries.relevance_annotation: Documents the evidence trajectory (2004 insufficient -> 2013 B -> 2018/2025 updates) that T-PHE's programme theory should be read against; supports treating IPV screening/referral guidance as an evolving, tier-honest evidence base rather than settled fact, consistent with the epistemic-humility safeguard.
entries.verifier_note: first_author is wrong: search record lists 'US Preventive Services Task Force' but PubMed indexes the first author as Moyer VA (writing on behalf of USPSTF; this is the standard citation form for this record, e.g. 'Moyer VA; U.S. Preventive Services Task Force'). Content of key_finding is fully supported by the abstract ('The USPSTF recommends that clinicians screen women of childbearing age for IPV...B recommendation...current evidence is insufficient to assess...all elderly or vulnerable adults...I statement'). FIX: change first_author to 'Moyer VA' (or 'Moyer VA, on behalf of the USPSTF').

entries.title: Screening for family and intimate partner violence: recommendation statement
entries.design: guideline / recommendation statement
entries.population_setting: US general population, family and intimate partner violence screening in primary care
entries.finding: USPSTF found the evidence insufficient (I statement) to recommend for or against routine screening instruments to detect domestic violence, updating a 1996 insufficient-evidence finding; explicitly states the letter grade reflects the quality and magnitude of evidence available at that time, not an assumption of no benefit.
entries.relevance_annotation: Historical baseline showing that even the narrow, well-resourced clinical screening literature took over a decade to accumulate evidence sufficient for a positive recommendation -- cautions against assuming a practitioner-led programme-theory synthesis like T-PHE has already crossed an analogous evidentiary threshold; relevant to epistemic humility (P1-adjacent) and the FAILURE CRITERION.
entries.verifier_note: Title, year (2004), journal (Annals of Internal Medicine), first_author all match. BUT the PubMed abstract for this record is purely procedural/administrative -- it describes the process ('In 1996, the USPSTF found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against...a grade C recommendation, according to 1996 grade definitions. The USPSTF now uses an explicit process...') and does NOT itself state the 2004 recommendation's actual grade or conclusion text (no 'I statement' or 'insufficient evidence' language about the 2004 finding appears in the abstract retrieved via efetch). The key_finding's specific claim ('USPSTF found the evidence insufficient (I statement) to recommend for or against routine screening instruments...') is historically well-established (corroborated indirectly by PMID 23338828's abstract, which refers to updating '2004' with a new B-grade) but is not directly supported by this record's own PubMed abstract text. FIX: either cite a source that states the 2004 grade explicitly, or soften key_finding to note the grade is inferred from the update history in PMID 23338828 rather than quoted from this abstract.

entries.title: Screening women for intimate partner violence: a systematic review to update the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendation
entries.design: systematic review (evidence base for USPSTF 2013 update)
entries.evidence_level: Systematic review underlying global guidance (USPSTF evidence report)
entries.population_setting: Women in health care settings, US-relevant evidence base
entries.finding: Of 15 fair/good-quality studies evaluating 13 screening instruments, 6 were highly accurate; 14 studies found minimal adverse effects from screening, though some women reported discomfort, loss of privacy, emotional distress, and fear of further abuse; counseling interventions reduced IPV/improved outcomes in some subpopulations (pregnant women, new mothers, family-planning clients) but a large trial found no significant screening-vs-usual-care difference overall.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly relevant to the STOP RULE and dignity/consent safeguard: names concrete harm categories from disclosure (loss of privacy, emotional distress, fear of further abuse) that a joint-couple education format could plausibly worsen, supporting P4 (private/confidential channel and the stop rule for suspected coercion).
