entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms attachment-based argument for conjoint treatment of situational couple violence (SCV, distinct from coercive control), safety plan/time-out strategy, and 'cautions for the appropriateness of couples counseling with ongoing violence.' Matches record.

entries.title: Women and men's use of coercive control in intimate partner violence.
entries.design: cross-sectional comparative study, n=172 (85 men, 87 women), self-report (CTS2 + modified PMWI)
entries.population_setting: community/convenience samples reporting on own and partner's IPV behavior
entries.finding: Coercive control was associated with IPV similarly for men and women across three samples, and was predominantly reciprocal — both partners commonly reported both receiving and perpetrating controlling behaviors, regardless of physical-abuse status.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates P4/the stop rule's implicit assumption of a clearly identifiable, typically unidirectional 'coercive control' pattern: measurement studies of general/community samples often find bidirectional reporting of controlling behavior, which is a known contested area in the field and a reason T-PHE needs an explicit, expert-informed assessment protocol rather than assuming coercive control is self-evidently detectable.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms n=172 (85 men, 87 women), coercive control associated with IPV similarly by gender, 'predominantly reciprocal in nature.' Matches record exactly.

entries.title: Psychometric Properties of the Coercion in Intimate Partner Relationships Scale.
entries.design: instrument-development/validation study
entries.population_setting: adult participants reporting on intimate relationships (validation sample)
entries.finding: Reports on validity/reliability of the Demand, Threat, Surveillance, and Response-to-Demands subscales of the Coercion in Intimate Partner Relationships (CIPR) scale, developed because existing coercive-control measures had documented content-validity gaps (not capturing the full range of demand/threat/surveillance tactics).
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports the STOP RULE / P4 operational need: shows a validated, multi-dimension instrument exists for identifying coercive control (demand, threat, surveillance), which T-PHE's 'confidential assessment' step would need to specify rather than leave undefined — a concrete gap in the current abstract.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms CIPR subscales (Demand, Threat, Surveillance, Response to Demands), rationale that 'content validity appears to be an issue for existing measures,' and validity/reliability support. Matches record.

entries.title: Validation of the Coercive-Composite Abuse Scale (C-CAS) in an Australian sample of women experiencing intimate partner abuse.
entries.design: instrument-development/validation study, n=854 adult women + qualitative survivor/expert feedback
entries.population_setting: Australian women, community survey sample
entries.finding: Developed and psychometrically tested a new self-report Coercive-Composite Abuse Scale (C-CAS) designed to capture severity, frequency and pattern of coercive control holistically, explicitly because prior measures showed 'limited understanding of these patterns of behaviour.'
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P2 (private channel makes concerns visible) and the stop rule's assessment step: a recent, patient/survivor-informed, psychometrically validated tool exists that T-PHE's confidential-assessment mechanism could adopt or cite, rather than relying on unstructured clinical judgment alone.
entries.verifier_note: Confirmed real PMID (2026, BMJ open, Hegarty) despite the unusually high 8-digit number for a record dated 2016-search-vintage-looking data — not a fabrication. Abstract confirms n=854 Australian women, C-CAS four-factor structure, developed because prior measures showed 'limited understanding of these patterns of behaviour.' Matches record.

entries.title: Coercive Control in the Courtroom: the Legal Abuse Scale (LAS).
entries.design: instrument-development study, n=222 survivor-mothers, exploratory factor analysis + Rasch analysis
entries.population_setting: US survivor-mothers involved in family law proceedings
entries.finding: Developed a 14-item, two-subscale Legal Abuse Scale (LAS) to measure how family-court and legal processes can be misused by partners to continue coercive control post-separation.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant to bounded authority and referral (P5) and repairability: illustrates that coercive control can persist through formal/legal systems after a couple separates, which is a downstream risk T-PHE's referral pathway and 'never resumes where coercive control is confirmed' rule should anticipate, especially for referral to legal/marital dissolution processes in a Thai/Muslim family-law context.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms n=222 survivor-mothers, EFA + Rasch analysis, 14-item two-subscale (Harm to Self/Motherhood, Harm to Finances) Legal Abuse Scale for legal-system misuse post-separation. Matches record.

entries.title: Development of a brief measure of intimate partner violence experiences: the Composite Abuse Scale (Revised)-Short Form (CASR-SF).
entries.design: instrument-development study using pooled secondary data from 5 Canadian studies, n=6,278 adult women; international expert Delphi-style item rating
entries.evidence_level: single psychometric development study (secondary data pooling)
entries.population_setting: Canadian adult women, pooled multi-study sample
entries.finding: Developed a brief, validated 15-item short form of the Composite Abuse Scale, addressing the problem that most IPV measurement 'privileges physical violence, with poor assessment of other experiences,' which had led to underestimating the scope of IPV in populations.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P2 (private channel makes concerns visible): a brief, low-burden, validated tool exists that could plausibly be embedded in a premarital private-channel step, but its short length is a known trade-off against fully capturing coercive-control experiences (see Evans 2016 below) — a design tension T-PHE has not addressed.
entries.verifier_note: Core finding is supported (15-item CASR-SF, pooled n=6,278 Canadian women, rationale that IPV measurement 'often privilege[s] physical violence, with poor assessment of other experiences'). Minor overreach: the record's 'design' field calls the expert input 'Delphi-style item rating' — the abstract describes '31 international IPV experts... rated CAS items via an online survey,' a single round, not an explicit Delphi (iterative multi-round consensus) method. Change 'Delphi-style' to 'expert panel survey' or similar to avoid implying a specific methodology not stated in the abstract.

entries.title: Evaluating the Chinese Revised Controlling Behaviors Scale.
entries.design: mixed-methods evaluation study, n=200 Chinese women survivors, in-depth interviews + ROC curve analysis
entries.population_setting: Chinese women survivors of intimate partner violence
entries.finding: Qualitative accounts of 91/200 women were consistent with Dutton and Goodman's coercive-control conceptualization; the Chinese Revised Controlling Behaviors Scale showed acceptable discriminative accuracy (reported via ROC/AUC) for identifying high-control relationships in a non-Western cultural sample.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly supports P3 (cultural tailoring helps only if culture cannot override consent/safety): demonstrates that Western coercive-control frameworks and instruments can be cross-culturally adapted and validated in an Asian setting, which is a relevant precedent for adapting assessment in the Thai Muslim/intercultural context T-PHE targets, while also showing this requires dedicated validation work, not an assumption of universality.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms n=200 Chinese women, 91/200 qualitative accounts consistent with Dutton and Goodman's coercive-control conceptualization, and strong discriminative accuracy (AUC=.99 split-half; 96%/95% sensitivity/specificity on holdout). Matches record; 'ROC curve analysis' framing accurate.

entries.title: "Even 'Daily' is Not Enough": How Well Do We Measure Domestic Violence and Abuse?-A Think-Aloud Study of a Commonly Used Self-Report Scale.
entries.design: qualitative think-aloud/cognitive interviewing study with a validated quantitative scale (Composite Abuse Scale)
entries.population_setting: women with experience of domestic violence and abuse
entries.finding: Think-aloud interviewing revealed systematic underreporting on a widely used, validated DVA scale, particularly for coercive control, threatening behavior, restrictions to freedom, and sexual abuse, driven by item-interpretation confusion, fear of answering truthfully, and reluctance to self-identify as abused.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates P2/the private channel and the stop rule's reliance on self-report or brief screening to trigger assessment: even validated instruments substantially undercount coercive control specifically, meaning a premarital private-disclosure channel cannot be assumed reliable for detecting the exact pattern the stop rule needs to catch, without additional safeguards (trained interviewer, repeated contact, non-leading framing).
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms think-aloud/cognitive interviewing on the Composite Abuse Scale, underreporting 'particularly of coercive control, threatening behavior, restrictions to freedom, and sexual abuse,' linked to item-interpretation confusion and fear/reluctance to disclose. Matches record.

entries.title: Examining strength at home couples to prevent intimate partner violence on a military installation: A randomized controlled trial.
entries.journal: Journal of consulting and clinical psychology
entries.design: randomized controlled trial, n=138 couples
entries.population_setting: US military service members and partners on a military installation
entries.finding: Service members randomized to the couples-based Strength at Home Couples (SAH-C) prevention program showed greater effect-size reductions than a comparison Supportive Prevention condition across physical, sexual, psychological, and specifically coercive-control IPV, plus greater reductions in suicidality; partner-reported effects were in the same direction but less robust.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P1 (governance layer/decision control) with an important caveat: this is the strongest empirical evidence in this angle's search that a structured couple-based group prevention programme can reduce coercive-control IPV specifically — but it is a targeted prevention trial with built-in risk protocols in a screened population, not premarital joint education for a general population as T-PHE proposes, so it does not license extrapolation to T-PHE's context without similar screening infrastructure.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms n=138 couples RCT, SAH-C vs Supportive Prevention, service-member reductions across physical/sexual/psychological/coercive-control IPV and suicidality, partner-reported effects 'in the same direction but not as robust.' Matches record; caveat about targeted/screened prevention population (not premarital) is appropriate and present in the record.

entries.title: Screening for Intimate Partner Violence, Elder Abuse, and Abuse of Vulnerable Adults: Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force.
entries.design: systematic review commissioned for USPSTF (global-level guidance body), 30 included studies
entries.evidence_level: systematic review for a global/national guideline body (USPSTF)
entries.population_setting: adults in healthcare settings, US and comparable settings
entries.finding: Concludes screening instruments can accurately identify IPV in health care settings and that some interventions (e.g., counseling) following screening among women of reproductive age reduce IPV; harms of screening were assessed and found to be low, informing a USPSTF grade-B recommendation for reproductive-age women.
entries.relevance_annotation: GLOBAL-level guidance supporting P5/the referral safeguard and the value of a structured screening-plus-response system: a USPSTF-commissioned systematic review is the highest-tier evidence in this record set that screening + appropriate referral (not joint treatment per se) is the evidence-supported public-health mechanism, which aligns with T-PHE's referral/accountability proposition more than with its joint-education component.
entries.verifier_note: PMID/title/year correct, but the key_finding materially overstates the abstract's conclusions in two ways. (1) The abstract's actual conclusion is: 'trials of IPV screening in adult women did NOT show a reduction in IPV or improvement in quality of life over 3 to 18 months' — screening tools were found to 'reasonably identify' IPV (accuracy claim only, sensitivity/specificity varied widely by tool), but the record's claim that the review found 'some interventions (e.g., counseling) following screening among women of reproductive age reduce IPV' is too broad: only 2 of 11 intervention RCTs (1 home-visiting, 1 multi-risk behavioral counseling) showed significant reduction, and only in PREGNANT women specifically, not the general reproductive-age population. (2) 'informing a USPSTF grade-B recommendation' conflates this article (the evidence report/systematic review, PMID 30357304) with the companion USPSTF Recommendation Statement, which is a SEPARATE PMID (30357305, also JAMA 2018;320(16):1678-1687) not cited in the record. Fix: rewrite key_finding to state the evidence report found screening tools moderately accurate but screening ITSELF did not reduce IPV/improve QoL in trials; only 2 specific interventions in pregnant-women subgroups showed benefit; and either cite PMID 30357305 separately for the actual grade-B recommendation or explicitly note this record is the evidence report underlying that recommendation, not the recommendation itself.

entries.title: A scoping review of intimate partner violence assistance programmes within health care settings.
entries.design: scoping review, 43 included studies
entries.population_setting: health care settings, multiple countries
entries.finding: Of 43 studies across 9 categories of IPV assistance programmes (counselling/advocacy, safety planning, referral, resource provision, home visitation, case management, videos, provider cueing, system changes), programmes using a single active-assistance type combined with a counsellor/advocate reported positive results in 77.8% of studies, suggesting simpler, advocate-led interventions outperform complex bundled ones.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P5 (referral quality = timeliness + accessibility + follow-through): evidence that referral/advocacy-based assistance (not joint couple treatment) is the intervention category with the most consistent positive results in healthcare-adjacent IPV response, reinforcing that T-PHE's referral safeguard, if built with a trained advocate/counsellor link, has stronger independent evidentiary support than the joint-education component itself.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 43 studies, 9 categories, single active-assistance type + counsellor/advocate combination associated with 77.8% and 83.3% of studies reporting positive results respectively. Matches record closely (record's framing that this 'outperforms complex bundled ones' is a fair paraphrase of the reported associational pattern, not a causal claim overreach).

entries.title: Intimate partner violence: counseling, community resources, and legal issues for IPV victims and perpetrators.
entries.design: clinical practice review
entries.population_setting: primary/family care settings
entries.finding: Describes RADAR (Remember to ask routinely, Ask directly in private, Document, Assess safety, Review options) as a structured clinical tool for identifying and responding to IPV, emphasizing private questioning, safety assessment (weapons, children, perpetrator risk), and advocacy-based referral requiring trained links to community resources.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly supports P2 (private channel) and P5 (bounded authority and referral): RADAR is a concrete, citable model for exactly the kind of confidential-assessment and referral pathway T-PHE's stop rule presupposes but does not itself specify; T-PHE could operationalize its own private-channel/referral safeguard by adapting a RADAR-like protocol rather than leaving the mechanism abstract.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms RADAR (Remember/Ask/Document/Assess/Review) tool description, private questioning, safety assessment (weapons, children, perpetrator risk), advocacy-model referral. Abstract additionally states explicitly 'Couples counseling by family physicians is contraindicated' — relevant context the record's relevance_to_tphe does not mention but does not misstate either; worth citing directly if the manuscript wants a strong contraindication quote.

entries.title: Health care interventions for intimate partner violence: what women want.
entries.design: qualitative interview study with pile-sort methodology, n=21 women
entries.population_setting: US women with past or current IPV history
entries.finding: Most women supported informational interventions and individual counseling; notably, only 9 of 17 who rated it felt couple's counseling was a good idea, with 7 explicitly reporting it was 'definitely not useful' — direct survivor preference data skeptical of couples-based response to IPV.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates the case for any joint couple work where IPV is present, and supports dignity/consent and affected-person-visibility safeguards: this is direct, survivor-voiced evidence (not proxy/clinician opinion) that a substantial share of women with IPV history do not want couples counseling as a response — directly relevant to why T-PHE's stop rule treats joint work as something to halt rather than adapt when coercion is suspected.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms n=21 women, pile-sort methodology, 9 of 17 rated couple's counseling a good idea with 7 'definitely not useful.' Matches record exactly, including exact counts.

entries.title: Improving Provider Readiness for Intimate Partner Violence Screening.
entries.design: pre-post quality improvement intervention study
entries.evidence_level: single pre-post quality-improvement study (no control group)
entries.population_setting: healthcare providers (nurses, physicians, social workers) at a US clinical site
entries.finding: An EMR-integrated brief IPV screening tool plus provider education plus an automated resource/referral telephone system was associated with measured improvement in provider readiness to screen (assessed via the Domestic Violence Health Care Provider Survey Scale, pre/post t-test).
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P5 (referral timeliness/accessibility) and bounded authority: shows that referral quality and screening readiness are trainable, measurable provider-level competencies, underscoring that T-PHE's practitioner-led safeguards (epistemic humility, bounded authority) require analogous structured training and system infrastructure, not intention alone.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms EMR-integrated screening tool + provider education + automated resource/referral system, DVHCPSS pre/post t-test, significant overall increase in screening readiness (p=.003). Matches record; 'no control group' caveat in record's evidence_level field is accurate (single-group pre-post design).

entries.title: Implementing Trauma-Informed Partner Violence Assessment in Family Planning Clinics.
entries.design: quasi-experimental single-group pretest-posttest + qualitative interviews (survey n=132 baseline, n=68 3-month retention; interviews n=35)
entries.evidence_level: single quasi-experimental implementation study with qualitative component
entries.population_setting: women aged 18+ at two US family planning clinics
entries.finding: A brief, trauma-informed, universal IPV/reproductive-coercion assessment and education intervention was implemented with 65% of women receiving at least one intervention element; the mixed-methods evaluation describes uptake and provider/patient experience of the assessment process.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P2 (private channel visibility) and dignity/consent safeguards: demonstrates a real-world, trauma-informed implementation model for universal (not targeted) private assessment embedded in a routine service encounter, which is structurally analogous to what T-PHE's private-channel safeguard within premarital education would need to replicate, including its retention drop-off (52% at 3 months) as a caution about follow-through.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 2 family planning clinics, n=132 baseline / n=68 at 3-month (52% retention, matching record's '52% at 3 months' caution), n=35 interviews, 65% receiving at least one intervention element. Matches record.

entries.title: Patient and provider barriers, facilitators, and implementation preferences of intimate partner violence perpetration screening.
entries.design: qualitative study — patient interviews (n=10) and provider focus groups (n=29)
entries.population_setting: US Veterans Health Administration patients and providers
entries.finding: Identifies convergent and divergent patient/provider beliefs about barriers and facilitators to screening specifically for IPV perpetration (not just victimization), an area with a much thinner evidence base than victimization screening.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant to P1 (decision control) and P4/stop-rule symmetry: highlights that screening for use of coercive control/violence (not only victimization) is understudied and operationally harder — a gap T-PHE's assessment mechanism would need to address for both partners, not only the presumed victim, especially given the coercive-control-reciprocity findings noted elsewhere in this record set (Robertson 2011).
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms n=10 patient interviews, n=29 provider focus groups, VHA setting, explicit framing that perpetration ('IPV use') screening has 'an extremely limited evidence-base' compared to victimization screening. Matches record.

entries.title: Approaches to screening for intimate partner violence in health care settings: a randomized trial.
entries.design: cluster randomized trial, n=2,602 eligible women across 6 clinical sites (emergency, family practice, women's health)
entries.population_setting: English-speaking women aged 18-64 in Ontario, Canada healthcare settings
entries.finding: Compared face-to-face interview, written self-completed questionnaire, and computerized screening for IPV to determine the optimal screening method in terms of accuracy, acceptability and completeness.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P2 (private channel design): direct trial-level evidence on which screening modality (interview vs. self-report vs. computerized) women find acceptable and complete, directly informing how T-PHE's private/confidential channel for surfacing concerns should be designed rather than assumed to work in any format.
entries.verifier_note: PMID/title/year/design details (n=2,602 eligible women, 6 Ontario clinical sites, cluster RCT) all match. However the record's key_finding only restates the study's OBJECTIVE ('compared...to determine the optimal screening method') rather than the actual RESULT. The abstract's actual finding: women preferred self-completed formats over face-to-face; computer-based screening did not increase detected prevalence; written screens had the fewest missing data; PVS and WAST had similar sensitivity (~49%/47%) and specificity (~94%/96%) against the CAS criterion standard. Fix: replace key_finding with the actual result (format preference + accuracy findings), not just the study aim, since as written the relevance_to_tphe claim ('directly informing how T-PHE's private/confidential channel... should be designed') is only earned by the actual result, not the restated objective.

entries.title: Factor structures for aggression and victimization among women who used aggression against male partners.
entries.design: cross-sectional psychometric comparison study, n=412 women (African American, Latina, White) who had used physical aggression against a male partner
entries.population_setting: US community sample of women who had recently used aggression against a male intimate partner
entries.finding: Compared the factor structure and psychometric performance of three widely used IPV measures (CTS2, SES, PMWI) for assessing women's own perpetration versus victimization, finding the factor structure of women's perpetration differed from that of their victimization.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates a simple unidirectional coercive-control model underlying the stop rule: shows that standard IPV instruments do not measure perpetration and victimization symmetrically even within the same person, reinforcing that any assessment tool T-PHE's stop rule relies on must be validated for the specific direction/role being assessed, not assumed generalizable.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms n=412 (African American, Latina, White) women who had used aggression against a male partner, comparison of CTS2/SES/PMWI factor structures, finding perpetration model 'performed poorly in assessing women's sexual aggression, coercive control, and jealous monitoring' while victimization model performed well across factors. Matches record; the asymmetry finding is accurately characterized.

entries.title: Development and validation of a reproductive autonomy scale.
entries.design: Instrument development and validation (cross-sectional survey, factor analysis)
entries.evidence_level: Validation Study (single time-point, no longitudinal outcome data)
entries.population_setting: 1,892 women at 13 family planning and 6 abortion facilities, USA
entries.finding: Generated 26 candidate items, retained 14 items across 3 subscales (freedom from coercion, communication, decision-making) via factor analysis; the freedom-from-coercion and communication subscales were inversely associated with unprotected sex in the past 3 months, supporting construct validity.
entries.relevance_annotation: Foundational instrument for T-PHE's core construct of 'decision control' (P1); the 3-subscale structure (coercion-freedom, communication, decision-making) maps closely onto T-PHE's proposed outcome domains of informed choice and coercion recognition. Supports P1/P7 by showing decision control is measurable, not just conceptual.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 26-item pool -> 14 items retained across 3 subscales (freedom from coercion; communication; decision-making); construct validity via mixed-effects model where freedom-from-coercion and communication subscales were inversely associated with unprotected sex in past 3 months. Quote: 'Construct validity was demonstrated by a mixed-effects model in which the freedom from coercion subscale and the communication subscale were inversely associated with unprotected sex in the past three months.' Relevance claim (foundational instrument for 'decision control', measurable not just conceptual) is appropriately hedged, does not claim Thai/Muslim validity.

entries.title: Psychometric properties and refinement of the Reproductive Coercion Scale.
entries.design: Secondary psychometric analysis of pooled multicenter/RCT survey data
entries.evidence_level: finite_diagnostic (psychometric refinement on pooled RCT baseline data)
entries.population_setting: 4,674 women aged 16-29 in 24 Pennsylvania and 5 California family planning clinics, USA
entries.finding: Confirmed a 2-domain structure (pregnancy coercion, condom manipulation) and produced a validated 5-item short-form Reproductive Coercion Scale (RCS); recent reproductive coercion prevalence was 6.3-6.7% depending on the scale version used.
entries.relevance_annotation: Provides the field's most-used coercion-recognition instrument, directly relevant to T-PHE's coercion-recognition literacy outcome and the STOP RULE's premise that coercion must be identifiable/assessable rather than assumed absent. Supports P4/P5 (referral and stop-rule triggers need a measurable trigger construct).
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 2-domain structure (pregnancy coercion, condom manipulation), 5-item short-form RCS, and prevalence 6.7% (full) / 6.3% (short form) -- record's '6.3-6.7%' is accurate. Quote: 'Recent reproductive coercion was reported by 6.7% and 6.3% of the sample with the full and short-form RCS, respectively.' Relevance claim (coercion-recognition instrument for stop-rule trigger) is reasonable, no overclaim of Thai/Muslim applicability.

entries.title: Measuring social norms of intimate partner violence to exert control over wife agency, sexuality, and reproductive autonomy: an item response modelling of the IPV-ASRA scale.
entries.design: Item response modelling (Partial Credit Model) on population-based dyadic survey
entries.evidence_level: finite_diagnostic (single cross-sectional dyadic sample, non-Asian setting)
entries.population_setting: 559 married adolescent-girl-husband dyads (ages 13-18 wives), rural Niger, 2019
entries.finding: A 5-item, 2-dimensional social-norms scale (challenging husband authority; general IPV acceptability) showed reliability and validity; higher 'challenging husband authority' scores were statistically associated with husband perpetration of IPV.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly on-point setting (married adolescent couples, patriarchal marital governance) for T-PHE's claim that marriage is a governance threshold (core premise) and that norms legitimizing partner control over a wife's agency/sexuality are measurable and linked to violence risk. Supports P1 and the STOP RULE's rationale, though evidence comes from a very different (West African, non-Muslim-specific) cultural context, so cultural transfer to Thai Muslim/intercultural couples (P3) is not established.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 5-item, 2-dimensional Partial Credit Model (challenging husband authority; general IPV acceptability dimension), n=559 married adolescent-girl-husband dyads, rural Niger, 2019, and that higher 'challenging husband authority' scores were statistically associated with husband IPV perpetration. Quote: 'Higher scores on the "challenging husband authority" dimension were statistically associated with husband perpetration of intimate partner violence.' Relevance claim explicitly flags the non-Asian, non-Muslim-specific context as a limit on transfer to P3 -- appropriately hedged.

entries.title: Reproductive Coercion among Intimate Partner Violence Survivors in Nairobi.
entries.design: Mixed-methods (exploratory factor analysis, n=327; in-depth interviews, n=30)
entries.population_setting: Recent IPV survivors, informal settlements, Nairobi, Kenya
entries.finding: The US-developed Reproductive Coercion Scale transferred reasonably well to the Kenyan context, retaining a 2-factor structure (pregnancy coercion, condom manipulation; alpha=0.86); 82% of IPV survivors reported some reproductive coercion.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates T-PHE's implicit assumption that Western-validated decision-control/coercion instruments can be applied unmodified: even a successful transfer required explicit psychometric re-testing and qualitative recontextualization. Relevant to P3 (cultural intelligibility) — cross-cultural transferability of coercion constructs cannot be assumed, it must be tested, a gap T-PHE has not yet addressed for Thai Muslim/intercultural couples.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 2-factor solution (pregnancy coercion, condom manipulation, alpha=0.86) and 82% RC prevalence among IPV survivors. Quote: 'Psychometric analyses indicated a two-factor solution comprising pregnancy coercion and condom manipulation (alpha = 0.86). Eighty-two percent of IPV survivors reported experiencing RC.' Relevance claim correctly frames this as a caution against assuming unmodified transferability -- appropriate, not overstated.

entries.title: Reproductive coercion, gender role attitudes and fertility desire among married women in Türkiye: a descriptive and explanatory study.
entries.design: Cross-sectional descriptive-correlational survey with path analysis
entries.population_setting: 480 married women aged 18-49, Türkiye
entries.finding: Used the Reproductive Coercion Scale, Fertility Desire Scale, and Gender Roles Attitude Scale together; reproductive coercion and traditional gender-role attitudes were linked to fertility desire pathways in married women (path analysis).
entries.relevance_annotation: A Muslim-majority-country application of a validated coercion instrument specifically among married women, closer analogically to T-PHE's Thai Muslim/intercultural-couple setting than the US-origin studies. Supports P1/P2 by showing gender-role attitudes and reproductive coercion are jointly measurable within marriage in a Muslim-majority population, though it is descriptive/correlational, not evaluative of any education intervention.
entries.verifier_note: Title/year/design/population match exactly. PROBLEM: key_finding claims 'reproductive coercion and traditional gender-role attitudes were linked to fertility desire pathways' via path analysis, but the abstract's Results section only reports a path-analysis link between the Reproductive Coercion Scale and Fertility Desire Scale (r=0.172, p<0.001; beta=0.205, p=0.008) and does NOT report a statistically established gender-role-attitude -> fertility-desire path -- the Gender Role Attitude Scale is only mentioned as a measure administered (mean score 121.92+/-15.14), not as part of a reported path result. FIX: rewrite key_finding to state only the RCS-FDS path-analysis association (weak positive, r=0.172/beta=0.205) and drop or explicitly qualify the gender-role-attitudes-linked-to-fertility-desire claim as not shown in the abstract.

entries.title: Validation of a measure to assess decision-making autonomy in family planning services in three low- and middle-income countries: The Family Planning Autonomous Decision-Making scale (FP-ADM).
entries.design: Psychometric validation on cross-sectional multi-country survey data
entries.evidence_level: finite_diagnostic (multi-country validation, no Southeast Asian or Muslim-specific subsample)
entries.population_setting: Women in Argentina (n=890), Ghana (n=1,114), and India (n=1,130)
entries.finding: Adapted the Mothers Autonomy in Decision-Making (MADM) scale to contraceptive counselling contexts, producing the FP-ADM scale, and validated its psychometric properties across three culturally distinct LMIC settings including a South Asian one (India).
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly supports P1 (governance layer adds decision control beyond content/knowledge) by providing a validated instrument for autonomy specifically in the moment of a reproductive-health decision, and demonstrates such instruments can be adapted across culturally distinct settings including a South Asian population, relevant to Thailand's regional/cultural proximity.
entries.verifier_note: key_finding is accurate: MADM adapted to FP-ADM, validated in Argentina (n=890), Ghana (n=1,114), India (n=1,130), two-factor solution ('Bidirectional Exchange of Information', 'Empowered Choice'), good internal consistency. PROBLEM: relevance_to_tphe claims India's inclusion is 'relevant to Thailand's regional/cultural proximity' -- India is South Asia, Thailand is Southeast Asia; this is a geographic overreach, not a supported cultural-proximity claim (no shared language family, religion-majority, or documented cultural closeness argued in the source). FIX: remove or soften the 'regional/cultural proximity to Thailand' framing; state only that a South Asian (not Southeast Asian, not Muslim-specific) LMIC subsample exists, without implying meaningful proximity to the Thai Muslim/intercultural target population.

entries.title: Adaptation and psychometric assessment of a sexual and reproductive empowerment scale in Arabic among refugee and non-refugee adolescent girls.
entries.design: 4-step cultural adaptation (cognitive interviews, cross-sectional administration n=339, confirmatory factor analysis)
entries.evidence_level: finite_diagnostic (adaptation study, sub-optimal fit reported honestly)
entries.population_setting: Refugee and non-refugee adolescent girls aged 11-17, Lebanon (Arabic-speaking, majority-Muslim region), including participants in an early-marriage intervention
entries.finding: A Western-developed sexual and reproductive empowerment scale was adapted to Arabic; the original 13-item, 4-domain model showed poor fit in confirmatory factor analysis, and even after iteratively removing 2 items, model fit remained sub-optimal for most domains.
entries.relevance_annotation: Complicates P3 (cultural tailoring helps only if culture cannot override consent/safety): even careful, staged cultural/linguistic adaptation of an empowerment/autonomy instrument in an Arabic-speaking, early-marriage-affected adolescent population did not achieve strong psychometric fit, warning against assuming decision-control instruments will translate cleanly to a Thai Muslim setting without local validation work.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 13-item, 4-domain original model showed poor CFA fit; after removing 2 items, properties improved but were 'not optimal'; only the self-efficacy domain was 'acceptable'. Quote: 'The original model for the 13-item, four-domain adapted scale demonstrated poor fit in CFA. After iteratively removing two items, scale properties were improved, albeit were not optimal. The validity and reliability results for the self-efficacy domain were acceptable.' Record's 'sub-optimal for most domains' is consistent (3 of 4 domains not optimal). Relevance claim (warns against assuming clean cultural transfer) is appropriately cautious, not overstated.

entries.title: Turkish adaptation of the reproductive autonomy scale: Validity and reliability study.
entries.journal: The Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research
entries.design: Cross-cultural adaptation and psychometric validation (online survey, EFA/CFA)
entries.population_setting: 308 married women of reproductive age (15-49), Türkiye, recruited via WhatsApp/Instagram
entries.finding: The Reproductive Autonomy Scale retained its 3-subscale (14-item) structure in Turkish; subscale Cronbach's alpha ranged from 0.64-0.92 (total scale 0.66), with the decision-making subscale showing the lowest reliability among subscales tested.
entries.relevance_annotation: Another Muslim-majority-country adaptation of the RAS specifically in married women, supporting P1's premise that decision control is measurable within an established marriage. The comparatively lower reliability of the decision-making subscale (0.64) is a caution for T-PHE's proposed outcome measurement — the decision-control construct itself may be the hardest component to measure reliably across cultures.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 14 items/3 subscales and four alpha values (0.66 total, then 0.64, 0.89, 0.92) with test-retest high correlation. PROBLEM: the abstract does NOT state which named subscale (decision-making / freedom-from-coercion / communication) corresponds to the 0.64 alpha value -- it lists 'reproductive autonomy scale (RAS) total and subscale ... 0.66, 0.64, 0.89, and 0.92, respectively' without labeling order. The record's specific attribution 'the decision-making subscale showing the lowest reliability' is therefore NOT confirmed by the abstract alone. FIX: either verify against the full text which subscale=0.64 and cite that specifically, or soften to 'one subscale showed markedly lower reliability (alpha=0.64); the abstract does not specify which subscale this is' -- do not name 'decision-making' without full-text confirmation, since this is exactly the kind of psychometric-number precision this review is asked to be strict on.

entries.title: The Reproductive Autonomy Scale: German validation and application in an Austrian student population.
entries.design: Cross-cultural validation study
entries.population_setting: Austrian student population (including men)
entries.finding: The RAS 3-factor structure was supported; decision-making and freedom-from-coercion subscales had satisfactory internal consistency, while the communication subscale showed marginally lower reliability; use in men and gender-diverse individuals was noted as constrained, requiring adaptation.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P1's general claim that decision-control constructs are cross-culturally measurable, but flags that these instruments (like most reproductive autonomy scales) were built for women and are not readily applicable to male partners — relevant since T-PHE's programme theory addresses couples, including the male partner's role in enabling or constraining the other's decision control.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 3-factor structure supported; decision-making and freedom-from-coercion subscales 'satisfactory' internal consistency; communication subscale 'marginally lower reliability'; use in men/gender-diverse individuals flagged as constrained, requiring adaptation. Quote: 'Internal consistency of the subscales for decision-making and freedom from coercion was satisfactory, while the communication subscale showed marginally lower reliability... its use in men and diverse individuals is constrained, necessitating adaptations.' Here (unlike PMID 38339841) the subscale-specific attribution IS explicit in the abstract, so this record's specificity is warranted. Relevance claim about male-partner applicability is reasonable and directly useful to T-PHE's couple-level framing.

entries.title: Evaluation of the psychometric properties of the Reproductive Autonomy Scale for use in the UK.
entries.design: Cross-sectional online survey validation (classical test theory + CFA)
entries.population_setting: 826 women of reproductive age, United Kingdom
entries.finding: The RAS was highly acceptable (>97.7% response rate) with good internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha 0.75) and fair-good test-retest reliability (ICC 0.67); construct validity was supported via confirmatory factor analysis.
entries.relevance_annotation: Further supports P1 that reproductive/decision autonomy is a measurable, transportable construct; useful comparator baseline for any future Thai/Muslim-population adaptation T-PHE might pursue, but this population is culturally distant from the Muslim/intercultural Thai setting T-PHE targets.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms response rate >97.7%, Cronbach's alpha 0.75, test-retest ICC 0.67 ('fair-good'), and CFA-confirmed three-factor structure. Quote: 'Internal consistency was good, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.75. Test-retest reliability was fair-good with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.67... The three-factor structure of the scale was confirmed on confirmatory factor analysis.' Relevance claim explicitly notes the UK population is culturally distant from the Thai Muslim target -- appropriately hedged, not overstated.

entries.title: Development and Validation of the Sexual and Reproductive Empowerment Scale for Adolescents and Young Adults.
entries.design: Instrument development and validation (qualitative item generation + national survey, EFA, logistic regression)
entries.population_setting: 1,117 sexually active young people aged 15-24, USA (national sample)
entries.finding: Developed a 23-item, 7-subscale Sexual and Reproductive Empowerment Scale for Adolescents/Young Adults (including 'choice of partners, marriage, and children' as a named subscale); validation via logistic regression supported construct validity.
entries.relevance_annotation: The 'choice of partners, marriage, and children' subscale operationalizes almost exactly T-PHE's marriage-transition decision-control construct (proceed/delay/refuse marriage) for a younger cohort, giving a candidate measurement approach for P1/P7, though validated only in a US adolescent/young-adult sample, not Muslim or intercultural couples.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 23 items, 7 subscales, including 'choice of partners, marriage, and children' as a named subscale, and construct validity via logistic regression association with SRH information/service access. Quote: '23 items captured by seven subscales: comfort talking with partner; choice of partners, marriage, and children; parental support; sexual safety; self-love; sense of future; and sexual pleasure. Validation using logistic regression demonstrated that the subscales were consistently associated with sexual and reproductive health information and access...' Relevance claim is strong and directly on-point (this subscale most closely mirrors T-PHE's marriage-decision construct) and is correctly caveated as US adolescent/young-adult only, not Muslim/intercultural-couple validated.

entries.title: Construction and Validation of a Women's Autonomy Measurement Scale with Reference to Utilization of Maternal Health Care Services in Nepal.
entries.journal: JNMA; Journal of the Nepal Medical Association
entries.design: Scale construction and validation (24-item pool, psychometric testing, cross-validation across two districts)
entries.population_setting: Women in Rupandehi and Kapilvastu districts, Nepal (South Asian, patriarchal marital-household context)
entries.finding: Produced a 23-item women's autonomy scale with strong psychometric properties (Cronbach's alpha 0.84, test-retest r=0.87, content validity ratio 0.8), validated specifically for South Asian household/marital decision contexts, showing good convergent and discriminant validity.
entries.relevance_annotation: A South Asian (culturally and regionally closer than US/European instruments), household-decision-power-focused autonomy scale, relevant to T-PHE's P1/P2 claims about decision control and its measurability within a patriarchal marital household structure comparable in some respects to intercultural Thai settings.
entries.verifier_note: Psychometric numbers in key_finding are accurate: Cronbach's alpha 0.84, test-retest r=0.87, content validity ratio 0.8, good convergent/discriminant validity -- all quoted directly from abstract. PROBLEM: relevance_to_tphe/key_finding both assert the scale is 'validated specifically for South Asian household/marital decision contexts' and is a 'household-decision-power-focused autonomy scale', but the abstract never describes the item content -- it defines the construct only as generic 'women's autonomy... relevance to developing countries' and its outcome anchor is maternal health care service utilization, not household/marital decision-making specifically. FIX: remove or soften 'household/marital decision contexts' -- state that the abstract does not disclose item content, so the household/marital-decision framing is an inference, not an abstract-confirmed fact; also soften 'South Asian' generalization since it was validated only in two districts of one country (Nepal), not South Asia broadly.

entries.title: A family planning clinic-based intervention to address reproductive coercion: a cluster randomized controlled trial.
entries.design: Cluster randomized controlled trial (ARCHES)
entries.evidence_level: Th_coqc-equivalent for medical evidence: cluster RCT (strongest design in this set), null primary-outcome result
entries.population_setting: 4,009 females aged 16-29 across 25 family planning clinics (17 clusters), USA
entries.finding: The universal education/counseling intervention (ARCHES) did NOT significantly reduce reproductive coercion (ARR 1.50, 95% CI 0.95-2.35) or partner violence (ARR 1.07, 95% CI 0.84-1.38) at 1-year follow-up, though it improved secondary outcomes such as recognition and self-efficacy.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly instructive for T-PHE's FAILURE CRITERION: a rigorously trialed, well-known couple/clinic-based education-and-counseling intervention improved intermediate awareness/self-efficacy measures without producing a statistically significant reduction in the actual coercion/violence outcome — the exact 'success on process, silent on the core outcome' pattern T-PHE's failure criterion is designed to flag. This complicates any optimistic reading of P1/P4 by showing education-plus-counseling alone is an insufficient governance mechanism in a comparable (though non-Muslim, non-Thai) context.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms non-significant primary-outcome effects: ARR 1.50 (95% CI 0.95-2.35) for reproductive coercion, ARR 1.07 (0.84-1.38) for partner violence, with significant secondary-outcome gains (knowledge of PV resources, self-efficacy). Quote: 'Intervention effects were not significant for reproductive coercion [adjusted risk ratio (ARR) 1.50 (95% confidence interval 0.95-2.35)] or partner violence [ARR 1.07 (0.84-1.38)]. Intervention participants reported improved knowledge of partner violence resources... and self-efficacy...' Minor omission (not an error): abstract also reports a moderation finding that higher baseline coercion predicted a coercion decrease at T3 among the highest-risk subgroup -- record does not mention this nuance but its core claim is accurate as stated. 'ARCHES' trial-name label is not itself in the abstract but is the well-established public name for this Miller et al. 2016 trial; not a factual problem. Relevance claim (illustrating the 'success on process, silent on core outcome' failure pattern) is accurate and well-matched to T-PHE's failure criterion.

entries.title: Adolescents' Help-Seeking Behavior and Intentions Following Adolescent Dating Violence: A Systematic Review.
entries.design: Systematic review (19 studies)
entries.evidence_level: finite_diagnostic (systematic review, but of heterogeneous primary studies)
entries.population_setting: Adolescent victims of dating violence, mixed international samples (English-language literature)
entries.finding: Adolescents overwhelmingly favored informal help sources (friends most common) over formal services; females were generally more likely than males to seek help (with inconsistencies); measurement and definitions of both violence and help-seeking varied substantially across included studies, limiting comparability.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant to P5 (referral quality = timeliness + accessibility + follow-through): if the modal help-seeking behavior in violence-affected relationships is informal disclosure to peers rather than professional referral, T-PHE's referral pathway (private channel -> accountable referral) must actively compete with, or connect to, informal disclosure norms, not assume formal referral is the default route. Also flags a genuine measurement gap (inconsistent help-seeking definitions) directly relevant to how T-PHE would eventually need to operationalize 'safe help-seeking' as an outcome.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms 19 studies reviewed; informal sources (friends) most common; females generally more likely to seek help with inconsistencies; measurement/definition variation across studies limiting comparability. Quote: 'Adolescents were more likely to go to informal sources of support, with friends being the most commonly reported source. The majority of studies found females were more likely than males to seek help; however, inconsistencies in gender differences emerged. The variation in measurement and definition of ADV and help seeking included in this review impacts on its conclusions.' Relevance claim to P5 (referral must compete with/connect to informal disclosure norms) is reasonable and well-supported.

entries.title: Development and Testing of a Community-Based Intervention to Address Intimate Partner Violence among Rohingya and Syrian Refugees: A Social Norms-Based Mental Health-Integrated Approach.
entries.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
entries.design: Co-designed, two-phase community-based intervention (workshops); RCT-labelled but abstract available describes intervention development/testing
entries.evidence_level: finite_diagnostic (intervention development/testing report; effectiveness outcome not detailed in abstract)
entries.population_setting: Rohingya (Muslim minority, displaced) in Malaysia and Syrian refugees (Muslim-majority) in Lebanon
entries.finding: A social-norms-based, mental-health-integrated community intervention was co-designed with Rohingya and Syrian refugee communities specifically to reduce IPV and encourage help-seeking, using culturally embedded workshop delivery rather than clinical/individual counseling alone.
entries.relevance_annotation: Highly relevant population match for P3 (cultural intelligibility) and P4/STOP RULE: this is one of the few studies working directly with Muslim (Rohingya, Syrian) populations on IPV-related help-seeking, using a co-designed, community/social-norms approach rather than a top-down curriculum — supports T-PHE's premise that safeguards must be culturally intelligible and community-embedded, though it evaluates a broader community intervention, not a premarital-education governance layer specifically.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms co-designed, two-phase, social-norms/mental-health-integrated community workshop intervention with Rohingya (Malaysia) and Syrian (Lebanon) communities to reduce IPV and encourage help-seeking. Quote: 'To reduce IPV and encourage help-seeking, a two-phase community-based intervention was co-designed with Rohingya in Malaysia and Syrians in Lebanon. Three day workshops, utilizing a social norms-based mental health-integrated approach, were implemented...' Abstract text available was truncated before effectiveness results, and the record's own evidence_level note ('effectiveness outcome not detailed in abstract') correctly flags this limitation rather than overclaiming an effect. Population match to P3 (Muslim minority/majority populations) is accurate and relevance framing appropriately notes it is a broader community intervention, not premarital education specifically.

entries.title: Screening for coercive control with refugee women accessing settlement services.
entries.design: Program evaluation (SAHAR study): screening tool implementation with lived-experience panel consultation, focus groups, manager interviews
entries.evidence_level: finite_diagnostic (single-site program evaluation, qualitative + descriptive screening results)
entries.population_setting: 312 refugee women accessing settlement services, Australia (culturally tailored screening)
entries.finding: A culturally tailored coercive-control screening strategy (ACTS tool, assessing controlling behaviour, fear, threats, and physical abuse) was implemented with refugee women in settlement services, informed by a lived-experience panel; the study reports screening results and qualitative service/manager feedback on culturally tailored delivery.
entries.relevance_annotation: Directly supports the operational logic of T-PHE's STOP RULE and bounded-authority/referral safeguard: it demonstrates a real-world, culturally tailored coercive-control screening protocol for a comparable at-risk migrant/refugee population, with a lived-experience governance layer (panel input) analogous to T-PHE's participant-visibility safeguard. Useful evidence that structured coercive-control screening is operationally feasible pre-referral, though it is a screening/service-access study, not a premarital-education programme evaluation.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms SAHAR study, ACTS screening tool (controlling behaviour, fear, threats, physical abuse), n=312 refugee women, Australian settlement services, lived-experience panel consultation plus focus groups/manager interviews. Quote: 'The Safety and Health After Arrival (SAHAR) study tested a culturally tailored IPV screening and response strategy for refugee women accessing Australian settlement services... consultations with a lived experience panel and services, screening results, focus group data and manager interviews.' Relevance claim to the STOP RULE/screening-feasibility logic is reasonable and correctly scoped as screening/service-access, not a premarital-education evaluation.

entries.title: Person-centered abortion care scale: Validation for medication abortion in the United States.
entries.design: Sequential scale adaptation and validation (item generation, cognitive interviews n=12, survey N=182, EFA)
entries.evidence_level: Validation Study (single-country adaptation of a global-South-origin scale)
entries.population_setting: Medication abortion patients (telemedicine and in-person), USA; scale originally developed in Kenya (global South)
entries.finding: Adapted and validated a US Person-Centered Abortion Care (PCAC) scale with 3 subscales (Respect and Dignity, Responsive and Supportive Care, and a third partial subscale) from a global-South-originated instrument; 29 items retained via exploratory factor analysis.
entries.relevance_annotation: Relevant to T-PHE's dignity-and-consent safeguard: this is a validated instrument for measuring whether a reproductive-health-adjacent service was delivered with respect, dignity, and responsiveness from the recipient's own perspective — directly analogous to the kind of 'was the participant's dignity/consent honored' outcome T-PHE's safeguard framework implies but does not yet operationalize with a specific instrument.
entries.verifier_note: Design, population, and item counts are correct: 29 items, exploratory factor analysis, adapted from a Kenya-originated global-South instrument. PROBLEM: the third subscale is misnamed. The abstract explicitly names all three subscales: '(1) Respect and Dignity (10 items), (2) Responsive and Supportive Care (nine items...), and (3) Communication and Autonomy (10 items...)' -- the record's key_finding calls the third one only 'a third partial subscale', which is vague and inaccurate (it is not obviously 'partial' -- it has a full 10-item core, with one added mode-specific item, similar to subscale 2). FIX: rename to 'Communication and Autonomy (10 items, plus one additional telemedicine-specific item)' instead of 'a third partial subscale'.

entries.title: Reproductive Coercion and Relationship Abuse Among Adolescents and Young Women Seeking Care at School Health Centers.
entries.design: Secondary cross-sectional analysis of baseline survey data
entries.population_setting: 550 sexually active female high school students, USA (school health center attendees, ages 14-19)
entries.finding: 12% reported recent reproductive coercion and 17% reported adolescent relationship abuse; both were associated with differences in care-seeking and sexual health behaviors, measured via validated RC and relationship-abuse instruments.
entries.relevance_annotation: Supports P1/P5 by showing reproductive coercion and relationship abuse can be measured concurrently with care-seeking behavior in a school-based (education-adjacent) setting, structurally analogous to T-PHE's premarital-education setting, though the US high-school population is culturally and developmentally distinct from the marrying Muslim/intercultural adult couples T-PHE targets.
entries.verifier_note: Prevalence numbers are correct (12% recent RC, 17% ARA) among 550 sexually active female students. PROBLEM: key_finding claims 'both were associated with differences in care-seeking and sexual health behaviors' -- but the abstract EXPLICITLY states the opposite for reproductive coercion alone: 'There were no observed significant differences in care-seeking behaviors among those with recent reproductive coercion compared with those without.' It is adolescent relationship abuse (ARA), not reproductive coercion, that was associated with a care-seeking difference (increased odds of STI testing/treatment, aOR 2.08); the combined ARA+RC-exposed group showed differences in sexual-partner/contraception behaviors, not general 'care-seeking'. FIX: rewrite key_finding to state that RC alone showed NO significant care-seeking difference, ARA alone was associated with increased STI-testing care-seeking (aOR 2.08), and the ARA+RC combined group showed elevated odds of specific risk behaviors (older partner, more partners, hormonal-only contraception) -- do not state both constructs were 'associated with differences in care-seeking'.

entries.title: Wounded Healers: Exploring Coping With Intimate Partner Violence Among Health Care Workers in Malaysia.
entries.design: Qualitative in-depth interviews (n=6)
entries.population_setting: Health care workers who were IPV survivors, tertiary hospital, Malaysia
entries.finding: Six HCW-survivors used varied coping strategies (seeking help, spirituality, avoidance, self-harm, staying/leaving); survivors relied mainly on coworkers and sought formal help only when situations became critical, hindered by misconceptions about IPV, privacy concerns and fear of workplace gossip.
entries.relevance_annotation: P2 (private channel makes concerns visible) / P5 (referral timeliness and accessibility) - supports the case that informal disclosure precedes formal help-seeking and that stigma/privacy fears are real barriers T-PHE's confidential channel and bounded-authority referral safeguard must address; also useful evidence base for the 'safe help-seeking' outcome domain in the FAILURE CRITERION.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms all elements verbatim: 6 HCW-survivors, coping strategies list, reliance on coworkers, formal help only when critical, barriers = misconceptions/privacy/workplace-gossip fear. Malaysia, PubMed-indexed. No overstatement.

entries.title: Technology Access and Attitudes Toward Intimate Partner Violence: Evidence From a National Survey in Thailand.
entries.design: Cross-sectional national survey, binary probit regression
entries.population_setting: General population, national survey, Thailand (Muslim identity modeled as a covariate)
entries.finding: Muslim identity, poverty, and residence in southern/central Thailand correlated with higher IPV tolerance for both genders; internet access (as distinct from device ownership) significantly reduced IPV tolerance, suggesting a role for information access in shifting attitudes.
entries.relevance_annotation: P1/P6 (coercion-recognition and informed-choice outcome domain) - complicates: documents higher IPV-tolerance attitudes correlated with Muslim identity and southern/central Thailand residence at national-survey level, which is the population-level backdrop T-PHE's coercion-recognition literacy aim addresses; supports the FAILURE CRITERION's distinction between attendance/satisfaction and actual attitude/literacy change.
entries.verifier_note: Record status is 'Publisher' (ahead-of-print, PubDate 2026-06-16), so 2026 is correct, not a typo. Abstract: 'Muslim, poverty, and residence in southern/central regions correlate with higher IPV tolerance for both genders... internet access significantly reduces it' - matches key_finding exactly. National Thailand survey, in scope.

entries.title: Maternal victimization and neglected offspring: Child marriage, IPV and depression symptoms among Salar Muslim women.
entries.design: Cross-sectional, random-effects Poisson regression (n=201)
entries.population_setting: Married Salar (Turkic-Muslim minority) women, rural China
entries.finding: Among 201 married Salar Muslim women, 65.6% reported past-year child neglect, 30.8% reported past-year IPV, and 37.6% had experienced child marriage; child marriage and IPV victimization were associated with downstream child-neglect risk.
entries.relevance_annotation: P1/P4 (decision control and STOP RULE) - supports: shows a documented pathway in a Muslim minority population from child marriage through IPV to intergenerational harm, reinforcing why T-PHE frames marriage entry as a governance threshold requiring decision control and a coercion/violence stop rule rather than treating marriage completion as automatically protective.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'reported a 65.6% rate of child neglect and a 30.8% rate of IPV in the past year. 37.6% experienced child marriage... significant associations between child neglect and child marriage, IPV, and depression symptoms.' All three percentages and the association claim match exactly. Correctly identified as rural China (Salar Muslim minority), not Southeast Asia -- relevance framing does not overstate region.

entries.title: Child Marriage in South Asia: A Systematic Review.
entries.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
entries.design: Systematic review (PRISMA, 13 included studies of 520 screened), PROSPERO CRD42020190410
entries.population_setting: South Asian populations (India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka), including Muslim subgroups
entries.finding: Consistent correlates of child marriage were rural residence, low education, poor economic background, low mass-media exposure and religion (Hindu and Muslim in particular countries); downstream maternal-health effects included lower antenatal care use, institutional delivery and skilled birth attendance.
entries.relevance_annotation: P7 (repairability) / FAILURE CRITERION - supports the broader evidence base that child/early marriage clusters with reduced maternal-health-service use, relevant to why T-PHE frames reproductive-health literacy (not just knowledge/attendance) as a required outcome domain; regional (South Asia, not Southeast Asia) so context-adjacent rather than direct.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'Factors consistently associated with child marriage in South Asia were rural residence, low level of education, poor economic background, low exposure to mass media and religion... low utilization of antenatal care services, low institutional delivery, and low delivery assistance by a skilled birth attendant.' Matches key_finding closely. Record's own relevance text honestly flags 'regional (South Asia, not Southeast Asia) so context-adjacent rather than direct' -- no overstatement of geographic fit.

entries.title: Factors influencing sexual and reproductive health of Muslim women: a systematic review.
entries.design: Systematic review, narrative synthesis (59 studies, 22 countries)
entries.population_setting: Muslim women, multi-country (worldwide, including Southeast/South Asian settings)
entries.finding: Across 59 studies from 22 countries, many Muslim women had poor sexual and reproductive health (SRH) knowledge and negative attitudes shaping service access; religious and cultural beliefs, family and community were recurring barriers to contraception use and SRH service/information access.
entries.relevance_annotation: P3 (cultural tailoring helps only if culture cannot override consent/safety) / FAILURE CRITERION reproductive-health-literacy domain - supports: documents the global evidence base that cultural/religious framing shapes SRH knowledge gaps in Muslim populations, which is the literacy gap T-PHE's failure criterion targets as a required outcome distinct from attendance/satisfaction.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: '59 studies were included from 22 countries... Many Muslim women have poor SRH knowledge, and negative attitudes... Religious and cultural beliefs were barriers to contraception use and access to SRH services and information.' Matches key_finding. Global systematic review, in scope, relevance framing appropriately generic (not claimed Thailand-specific).

entries.title: A qualitative study on perceptions of adolescents' sexual and reproductive health education in Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
entries.journal: International Journal of Adolescent Medicine and Health
entries.design: Qualitative (focus groups and individual interviews, feminist analytic lens), fieldwork 2016
entries.population_setting: Javanese Muslim adolescents and adults, Yogyakarta, Indonesia
entries.finding: School-based SRH education in the Javanese Muslim community was constrained by taboo and moral-panic framing around premarital sex; delivery gaps left adolescents without reliable sexuality information despite peer-counsellor programmes intended to fill this role.
entries.relevance_annotation: P3 (cultural intelligibility vs consent/safety boundary) - complicates: shows that in a comparable Southeast Asian Muslim-majority setting, culturally cautious SRH-education framing can itself suppress the informed-choice/reproductive-literacy content T-PHE's failure criterion requires, illustrating the tension P3 explicitly flags (cultural tailoring must not override the substance of informed choice).
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'contentious due to societal and religious taboos... misunderstood as a potential catalyst for premarital sex... Peer counsellors... reproduced adult moral values toward their peers, leading to a reluctance among adolescents to share their issues. Consequently, SRH education failed to reach those experiencing unwanted pregnancy or a toxic intimate relationship.' Matches key_finding's taboo/moral-panic and peer-counsellor-gap framing precisely.

entries.title: Intimate Partner Violence among Canadian Muslim Women.
entries.design: Qualitative dominant design with supplemental quantitative data (n=8)
entries.evidence_level: Qualitative study with descriptive quantitative supplement
entries.population_setting: Canadian Muslim immigrant women, 6 countries of origin
entries.finding: Pre-migration adverse childhood experiences and family history of IPV, combined with post-migration language/social-isolation barriers and internalized patriarchal values, shaped help-seeking and the eventual decision to leave abusive relationships among 8 Muslim immigrant women.
entries.relevance_annotation: P1/P5 (decision control and referral quality: timeliness, accessibility, follow-through) - supports: documents concrete pre- and post-marriage barriers to disclosure and help-seeking in Muslim women, reinforcing why T-PHE frames accountable referral (not just availability) as a distinct success criterion from attendance/satisfaction.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms pre-migration ACEs/family IPV history, post-migration language/isolation barriers and internalized patriarchal values shaping help-seeking and the decision to leave. Population correctly stated as Canadian immigrant Muslim women (not Southeast Asia); relevance text does not claim regional fit, only thematic (help-seeking/decision-control) relevance.

entries.title: Muslim Women's Experiences of Domestic Violence and Abuse: A Meta-Ethnography of Global Evidence.
entries.design: Meta-ethnography (33 qualitative studies synthesized), 6 databases searched
entries.population_setting: Muslim women, global (multi-country qualitative evidence)
entries.finding: Synthesis of 33 qualitative studies identified four major themes - experience/impact of abuse, risk factors, help-seeking, and coping - and found religion functions both as a risk factor for abuse and a barrier to help-seeking, and simultaneously as a coping resource for some women.
entries.relevance_annotation: P1/P3/P5 (decision control, cultural intelligibility vs safety, referral quality) - supports: the dual role of religion (barrier and resource) directly substantiates T-PHE's epistemic-humility and cultural-intelligibility safeguards, and the help-seeking/coping themes ground the FAILURE CRITERION's coercion-recognition and safe-help-seeking outcome domains in Muslim populations specifically.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: '33 qualitative studies... four major themes: the experience and impacts of abuse; risk factors...; help-seeking; and the coping strategies... religion not only as a risk factor for violence and a barrier to help-seeking but also as a coping strategy.' Matches key_finding's 'four major themes' and dual-role-of-religion claim exactly.

entries.title: Shame, Family Honor, and Dating Abuse: Lessons From an Exploratory Study of South Asian Muslims.
entries.design: Exploratory qualitative study
entries.population_setting: South Asian Muslim communities (diaspora)
entries.finding: Cultural norms constructing dating as shameful were found to intensify fear of parental/community reaction and strengthen attachment to abusive partners, with direct implications for disclosure, help-seeking, and the ability to end abusive relationships.
entries.relevance_annotation: P4 (STOP RULE) / P1 (decision control) - supports: illustrates the mechanism by which family-honor and shame norms can suppress disclosure of coercion/abuse before or during a relationship transition, which is precisely the risk the STOP RULE (pause joint work pending confidential assessment) is designed to interrupt.

These then have implications for disclosure, help seeking, and ending abusive relationships.' Matches key_finding. Correctly labeled as South Asian Muslim diaspora, not Thailand/Southeast Asia.

entries.title: Establishing a one-stop crisis center for women suffering violence in Khonkaen hospital, Thailand.

entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'discusses the experiences of the Khonkaen provincial hospital, which has been selected as an intervention case site for a one-stop crisis service... compared with another provincial hospital where no intervention has taken place.' Matches key_finding directly. Thailand, PubMed-indexed, on-topic OSCC evidence.

entries.title: [Domestic violence as a women's health issue--activities of health professionals in Thailand].

The key_finding's 'in one case, a community religious leader (a Buddhist monk)' correctly hedges to a single case, not a general claim -- accurate, not overstated.

entries.title: "Hitting as Light as Feathers": Religious Leaders' Voices on Domestic Violence.

entries.title: An empirical exploration of female child marriage determinants in Indonesia.

entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'approximately 17% and 6% report being married before 18 and 16 years old respectively... Research on child marriage in Southeast Asia is scarce.' Matches key_finding's prevalence figures and the 'scarce prior research' framing exactly. Nationally representative Indonesia data, in scope.

entries.title: Marriage is not a safe place: heterosexual marriage and HIV-related vulnerability in Indonesia.

entries.population_setting: Married women, Indonesia (Muslim-majority context)
entries.finding: Traditional practices including polygamy, early marriage and contract marriage (mut'a) were identified as enhancing married Indonesian women's likelihood of HIV acquisition within marriage, challenging the assumption that marital status is protective.
entries.relevance_annotation: P1/P6 (conventional success can coexist with failure) - supports: directly substantiates T-PHE's proposition that marriage completion is not itself evidence of a good outcome; reproductive/health-literacy and safety risks can persist or increase after marriage in a Southeast Asian Muslim-majority setting, reinforcing the FAILURE CRITERION's separation of completion from literacy/safety outcomes.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'traditional practices such as polygamy, early marriage and contract marriage (mut'a) play an important role in enhancing women's likelihood of acquiring HIV within the Indonesian context.' Matches key_finding. Indonesia, in scope; relevance claim (marriage completion not evidence of good outcome) is a reasonable reading, not overstated.

entries.title: Cultural and religious determinants of HIV transmission: A qualitative study with people living with HIV in Belu and Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
