entries.population_setting: People living with HIV, Belu and Yogyakarta, Indonesia (Islamic and Javanese cultural context)
entries.finding: Cultural practices (bride wealth, spousal-dispute management) and Islamic religious beliefs about husband-wife relationships, forbidden premarital sex, and condom use were reported by participants as shaping spousal sexual behaviours that contributed to HIV transmission within marriage.
entries.relevance_annotation: P3 (cultural tailoring vs consent/safety boundary) / P6 - supports: provides Southeast Asian Muslim-context evidence that religious/cultural norms around marital sexuality can constrain safety-relevant negotiation (e.g. condom use) inside marriage, reinforcing why T-PHE requires cultural tailoring to stop short of overriding consent/safety-relevant informed choice.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'cultural practices in Belu related to the use of bride wealth, managing spousal disputes, marriage, and condom use... Islamic religious beliefs about expected husband-wife relationships, forbidden premarital sex, and... condom use... contributed to HIV transmission.' Matches key_finding. Indonesia, in scope.

entries.title: Regulation of sexuality in Indonesian discourse: normative gender, criminal law and shifting strategies of control.
entries.design: Historical/discourse review
entries.population_setting: Indonesia, state/religious/activist discourse, 1980-2000s
entries.finding: Traces how Indonesian state and Islamic discourse shifted from linking normative gender to heterosexual marriage toward more direct legal regulation of sexuality via criminal-code proposals, illustrating how marriage has functioned as a governance mechanism in national policy discourse.
entries.relevance_annotation: P1 (marriage as governance threshold) - supports contextually: provides historical/policy background on how marriage functions as a formal governance mechanism in a Southeast Asian Muslim-majority nation-state, background context for T-PHE's framing of the marriage transition as a governance threshold rather than a purely private event; not empirical outcome data.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract confirms the historical-discourse trajectory: New Order gender/heterosexuality-marriage linkage -> 1990s Islamic-discourse shifts -> post-1998 push for criminal-code restrictions on sexuality. Matches key_finding. Record's own relevance text correctly labels this 'not empirical outcome data,' avoiding overclaim.

entries.title: Prevalence of and factors associated with female child marriage in Indonesia.
entries.design: Cross-sectional, binary logistic regression (nationally representative, n=9,333)
entries.population_setting: Females aged 15-20, Indonesia (2017 Indonesia Demographic and Health Survey)
entries.finding: National prevalence of female child marriage in Indonesia was 12.53%; health insurance status and sex of household head were not significant predictors, while other socioeconomic/education factors were associated with child marriage risk.
entries.relevance_annotation: P1/P4 (governance threshold, STOP RULE) - supports: recent, nationally representative Southeast Asian baseline confirming that a meaningful proportion of marriages in the target region occur before full legal adulthood, underscoring why decision-control safeguards at the marriage-transition threshold remain a live concern rather than a historical one.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract: 'prevalence of female child marriage in Indonesia was quite high, reaching about 12.53%... health insurance and sex of household head did not significantly influence female child marriage.' Matches key_finding's prevalence figure and non-significant-predictors claim exactly. Nationally representative, in scope.

entries.title: Child Marriage Acceptability Index (CMAI) as an essential indicator: an investigation in South and Central Sulawesi, Indonesia.
entries.design: Cross-sectional survey, bivariate/ANOVA/logistic regression (n=1,000 households)
entries.population_setting: Households, Bone District (South Sulawesi) and Palu/Sigi/Donggala (Central Sulawesi), Indonesia
entries.finding: Household financial security, dowry practices and local legal frameworks were significantly associated with community acceptability of child marriage across two Indonesian provinces where child-marriage rates remain above the national average.
entries.relevance_annotation: P1 (governance threshold) / P3 (cultural tailoring vs safety) - supports: documents that community-level acceptability of child marriage (not just individual prevalence) persists in specific Indonesian regions, relevant evidence for why T-PHE frames the safeguard layer as needing to operate against prevailing local norms, not merely individual attitudes.
entries.verifier_note: Abstract supports: household financial security (p=0.016), dowry (p<0.001) and legal frameworks (p=0.017) as significant ANOVA-associated factors with child marriage acceptability in Bone/South Sulawesi and Palu-Sigi-Donggala/Central Sulawesi. However, the record's clause 'across two Indonesian provinces where child-marriage rates remain above the national average' is NOT supported for these specific study sites -- the abstract's '22 out of 34 provinces... above the national average in 2019' statement is a general national context sentence, not a claim tied to Bone/South Sulawesi or Central Sulawesi by name. FIX: change to something like 'two Indonesian provinces' and drop or separately attribute the 'above national average' clause as general Indonesia-wide context rather than a site-specific fact.

entries.title: Factors affecting child marriage and contraceptive use among Rohingya girls in refugee camps.

entries.title: Girl child marriage and the social context of displacement: a qualitative comparative exploration of Syrian refugees in Jordan and Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh.

entries.title: "What other option did I have?"- The effect of conflict and displacement on child marriage and early childbearing among displaced Rohingya adolescents.

entries.title: Women's autonomy and child survival: a comparison of Muslims and non-Muslims in four Asian countries.
